subsubtopic: PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to announce that at the request of the city of Windsor the federal government and the province of Ontario have agreed to undertake jointly a rental housing project in Windsor, pursuant to section 36 of the National Housing Act.
The project is in the final planning stages at the present time and will consist of approximately 200 three and four bedroom row housing rental units. This development is the fourth federal-provincial project in' the city; the previous projects produced 325 residential lots on which two rental housing projects have been constructed, producing 421 rental housing units. The cost of the project will be approximately $2,401,000, which will be shared 75 per cent by the federal government and 25 per cent by the province, or by the province and the municipality.
Tenders are expected to be called February 3 and work on the project will commence toward the end of the month. The project will provide immediate employment for about 100 construction workers, and as the units progress this figure is expected to rise to about 300.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to make an announcement which I am sure will interest members of the house. For some years now Canada has been one of the largest contributors to the United Nations relief and works agency for Palestine refugees. As you know, Mr. Speaker, this is a body established by the United Nations, and it has had the task of providing food, shelter and medical care as well as educational and rehabilitation facilities to the 930,000 Arab refugees who left their homes as a result of the hostilities which accompanied the establishment of the state of Israel in 1948 and 1949.
Opinions differ about the way in which the problem of these refugees should be settled, but there is general agreement on the need to assist them in the tragic plight in which they find themselves. UNRWA supplies its relief services to these unfortunate people at the amazingly small cost of $30 per refugee per year, but for some time the financial difficulties of the agency have been growing more and more desperate, despite very generous contributions by several countries, particularly the United States and the United Kingdom. Relief services, as I have already informed the house on an earlier occasion, are at subsistence level and recently have had to be cut, and the whole rehabilitation and educational program will have to be abandoned unless more funds are forthcoming.
I need hardly say that maintenance of this rehabilitation program is essential if there is ever to be a solution of the refugee problem. We informed the United Nations some weeks ago that our regular annual cash contribution of $500,000 would be made as usual for 1958-1959, subject to parliamentary approval, but the Secretary General of the United Nations is still appealing to all members of the United Nations to increase their contributions if they possibly can.

External Affairs
The government has accordingly decided to seek parliamentary approval, in supplementary estimates to be presented to the house in due course, for a special additional contribution to UNRWA for this year; and that contribution, subject to parliamentary approval, will be $1,500,000 worth of Canadian flour for the refugees. This represents about 20,000 tons of flour or approximately one million bushels of Canadian wheat.
We hope this substantial contribution of flour will encourage other countries to increase their contributions to UNRWA. Indeed, some have already announced such increases in response to the appeal of the Secretary General of the United Nations. I am sure the house will approve of this proposal. UNRWA and UNEF, the United Nations emergency force, in both of which we are interested, are important aspects of the efforts of the United Nations to establish conditions of peace and security in the Middle East.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, relating to an article in Maclean's magazine of February 1, written by Mr. Blair Fraser. I intend to refer to page 37, where a false statement occurs. It appears that this statement derives from an earlier similar false statement which appeared in the Hamilton Spectator of November 27, 1957. I should like to relate the two articles together and deal with them now.
In the Hamilton Spectator of November 27 there is an article written by Milford L. Smith, business editor of that newspaper, in which these two paragraphs appear, both of which are incorrect:
The Canadian trade delegation's proposal that British mills export tinplate and sheet steel to Canada brought protests today from Hamilton steel manufacturers that employment here would suffer.
This statement, Mr. Speaker, is incorrect. The Canadian trade delegation made no such proposal. A second statement, also incorrect in part, reads as follows:
Trade Minister Churchill was quoted as saying Canada now imports only one-tenth as much steel from Britain as it does from the United States-

Up to this point that statement is correct. The false part of it follows:
-and that there is a market in Canada for both sheet and tinplate.
That is incorrect, Mr. Speaker. I never made that statement.
In Maclean's magazine there occurs this paragraph on page 37.

subtopic: MR. CHURCHILL    REFERENCE TO ARTICLES IN HAMILTON "SPECTATOR" AND "MACLEAN'S" MAGAZINE

I should say at this point
that Mr. Blair Fraser's article is a good article dealing with the question of trade and contains a great deal of useful information, but he has fallen into error in this paragraph, which reads as follows:
Tinplate is an ironic example. When the Canadian trade mission visited a British steel plant in Wales, Gordon Churchill remarked that Canada was a potential market for tinplate.
I never made any such remark. I was aware that there was a surplus of tinplate in Canada, and at the same time there was a surplus of tinplate at the Margam steel works in Wales. This statement is completely and utterly false.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO CANADIAN ASSISTANCE TO WEST INDIES FEDERATION
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief interim reply to questions asked on January 11 and 20 by the hon. member for Assiniboia.

Inquiries of the Ministry The question asked by him is as follows, as reported at page 3195 of Hansard for January 11, 1958:
Can the Prime Minister inform the house of the results of the talks between officials of the new West Indian federation and the Canadian government relating to economic co-operation between the two nations? Was Canada asked for a loan or other economic assistance, and can the Prime Minister say what action Canada is considering to help the newest member of the commonwealth?
At that time I stated that I had not had an opportunity to review this matter with the officials. I am now able to say, Mr. Speaker, that this matter is under active consideration and it is hoped that in the very near future an announcement can be made indicating what steps this government proposes to take to give immediate evidence of Canada's willingness to help this new country, through such practical forms of assistance as may be appropriate. We shall also be giving consideration to more long-term measures of assistance. These matters will be drawn to the attention of the house in due course when consideration is somewhat further advanced. However, I should like to assure hon. members that most urgent study is being given to them.
I might also draw the attention of the house to the fact that a trade mission from Jamaica, one of the most important units or provinces in this new federation of the West Indies, is at present visiting Canada. The trade mission is led by Hon. Wills O. Isaacs, Jamaica's minister of commerce, and is made up of a number of prominent businessmen of that island who have come to Canada to explore ways in which the long-standing trade with Jamaica may be further developed and strengthened. This delegation will arrive in Ottawa on Saturday next; they will be received by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and subsequently will have discussions with ministers and officials in various departments. I also plan to spend some time with these visitors. Together we shall explore detailed ways in which the commercial ties between this important island in the Caribbean and ourselves can be strengthened.
It is by visits of trade missions such as this that new commercial contacts are found and the flow of trade broadened and deepened. I am sure that Canadians as a whole will welcome the visit of this Jamaican mission beginning on Saturday.

I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. This morning's Gazette carries the story of a speech made by the minister to the dominion marine association at the Seigniory club in the province of Quebec headed "Shipowners Greet Hees' Tolls Views". I quote just one short paragraph, which reads as follows:
Transport minister George Hees tonight told lake shipowners from both Canada and the United States his personal views on seaway tolls "are much in keeping with your own."
These views are that there should be a three to five year toll-free program on the seaway, and the question I wish to ask is this. Does the speech made by the minister indicate that consideration has been given to a three to five year toll-free operation period on the seaway?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY TOLLS    REPORTED STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. The statement I made was as follows, and I now quote from the text I used:
One matter in which I know you are very much interested is the tolls which will be charged when the seaway opens. This question is, unfortunately, at present under consideration by committees of both countries, and cannot, of course, be discussed here. I may say, however, that my personal views are much in keeping with yours, namely that the seaway will not be able to fulfil its purpose unless it is economically possible for a large volume of shipping to use it. The economy of Canada is very much dependent upon cheap water transportation.
Mr. Speaker, those were the views I expressed, and those were also the views expressed to me by various members of the dominion marine association who have visited me here in Ottawa during the past three months. They are views with which I thoroughly agree.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, January 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harkness for the second reading of Bill No. 237, to provide for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities, and the amendment thereto of Mr. McCullough.
(Translation):

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night, I was dealing with the psychological

aspect of this bill which provides for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities. I should now like to touch upon the practical aspects of this plan.
It is no exaggeration to say that the dairy industry is the backbone of Quebec agriculture. I might add that, in my own constituency, Roberval, it accounts for at least half of the total annual farm income. The support price of butter at 58 cents a pound has saved the farmers of my riding from bankruptcy. It has brought them a degree of security which, although it has not made them rich, has allowed them to pull through. The former St. Laurent government saw fit to support the price of butter at 58 cents a pound although at certain times 125 million pounds of it were in storage throughout the country and butter was selling at 38 cents a pound on the international market. May I congratulate the former minister of agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on his understanding of the problems of eastern farmers, and especially those in the province of Quebec when in 1955, at a time when he was considering to discontinue the support price for butter, because of a surplus in excess of a hundred million pounds, he yielded to the representations of a delegation from rural counties, of which I was a member, requesting that the support price be kept at the same level. Instead of letting that butter spoil in warehouses, the former government sold much of it on the international market and allowed our educational institutions and hospitals to take advantage of the international market price, 38 cents a pound. No sooner had the present government come to power than that privilege was withdrawn from those institutions, to their utter dismay and my own personal deep regret.
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
Under this bill, unless the new board of stabilization of agricultural prices uses other standards than the average price over the previous ten years, what will be the new guaranteed price for butter?
In 1957, the average price of first grade butter on the Montreal market was 60.6 cents a pound. According to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in the ten years prior to 1958, (that is from 1947 to 1957 inclusive) the average price of butter was 62 cents a pound. Under this bill,-if the board does not take into account other factors than the average price on a 10-year basis,- the guaranteed price of butter will be 49.6 cents a pound, 8.4 cents less than the support price granted by the former Liberal government under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. And if there should be a surplus of butter, as happened these last few years, farmers could count only on this guaranteed price of 49.6 cents a pound, and would have no alternative but to sell their herds as beef cattle and give up the none too prosperous dairy industry.
That is why I urge the government to give special consideration to the basis it will adopt in setting the floor price of butter, so that the price will not be lower than the 58 cent support price now in force. This is a matter of primary importance to the farm people of my constituency, whose interests it is my duty to protect.
According to figures supplied by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the 80 per cent average which is to be set as a guaranteed price for the following products would be these:

As this bill concerns the stabilization of farm prices by the establishment of guaranteed minimum prices set a year in advance, I would see in it the possibility of some security for the farmer if there was some relationship between the cost of the services required by the farmer-namely the price of farm implements and other farm equipment he has to buy as well as his labour costs- and the standards to be used in setting the
stabilization prices of farm products under this bill. That is why I really wonder about the advantages which this legislation would bring to the Canadian farmer. I realize it is by no means easy, at a time when agriculture is undergoing radical changes, to find a perfect solution to the difficult problem facing our agricultural class which, in our part of the country, is passing from the family stage
96698-233J

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization to the industrial stage, a change tor which our farmers are not all adequately prepared.
It would seem that, to face competition, our farmers will soon be forced to become something like managers of medium sized industrial concerns, and deal with such matters as market trends and production costs. Many of them, already, are clearly aware of those hard realities of our times. In my constituency in particular, with its growing number of progressive farmers, I have noticed a trend toward mechanization, development of larger farm areas and even specialization in a particular type of agricultural production, for instance poultry, hogs or eggs. It seems to me that those trends should not be ignored, and I believe it is time the agricultural loans' act were substantially improved for the benefit of farmers who wish to expand their farms and to make greater use of machinery so as to lower their operating costs as much as possible and also to encourage them to put on the market the finished products required by the consumer. All such capital expenditure requires funds beyond the means of the average farmer, however anxious he may be to keep up with the times.
Along with this last suggestion, I would like the industrial development bank to make its facilities more readily available to small industries in our agricultural communities, so as to open up local markets for our farmers. Not only would those small industries absorb a certain amount of agricultural manpower not at present interested in agriculture-therefore unwittingly overcrowding the farming profession-but would create jobs for those people.
It has always been my view that farming and industry should go hand in hand and that industry and farming in Canada will prosper only at such time as the farm worker can count on a yearly income comparable to that of the industrial worker, taking into account the particular obligations, risks and advantages in each group and profession.
As I like to believe in the good intentions of everybody, I am prepared to adopt this attitude towards the minister, whom I admire for piloting this far, with unruffled patience, so ungainly a bill, and I ask him in closing to avail himself wisely of the discretionary powers which are his under subsection 2 of clause 2 of this bill, if it passes, so that this legislation might serve the interests of farm people, as he expects it will. A 100 per cent farm legislation for an agricultural class 100 per cent worthy of the name, that is what I request for the farmers of my constituency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is too vitally important to the family farm everywhere in Canada to be allowed to pass in its present form. To the prairie regions, where agriculture is the main foundation of the economy, this will not only mean the end of the family farm as such, but it will mean depression to every community in that area. This is a fight for the rights of the working people, those people who toil with the sod to make a living for their families on their home property.
The rapid decline of the family farm across this nation can only be accurately described as desperate. The figures prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics illustrating the farmer's net income and gross income as compared with the rapidly rising costs of farming prove to any one who is willing to look at the situation that the farmer is lost in a cost-price squeeze. His position is desperate and requires remedial action, not just a palliative. There is something basically wrong with the position of agriculture in our economy, and measures must be adopted that will rectify the basic wrong.
I am not blaming the present government for the condition of agriculture, but it will be [DOT] blamed if it does not move rapidly to remedy the position. An analysis of the population of the prairie region at the present time shows with regard to those who were actually engaged in farming that approximately 12 per cent have left the farms in the past five years and about 10 per cent are still making a living though in many cases they are living on the depreciation of their farm machinery, while the rest are hanging on the ropes and cannot continue in their present condition for very long. These people are looking to this government to do something. They are justified in doing so because this government said it would take action to prevent the further decline of agriculture and improve its position in general.
The decline of agriculture under the previous government has left that industry in a desperate position. I believe the defeat of the previous government in the agricultural regions of Canada was largely due to the fact that that government had lost touch with the every-day problems of the toiling farmer. The previous administration completely failed to recognize the actual condition of the farmer.
I do not think this was ever better illustrated than during the past election in the province of Manitoba. The Winnipeg Free Press of May 20 carried a report of a public

meeting in a rural area in Manitoba which was attended by the former minister of trade and commerce, Right Hon. C. D. Howe. Mr. Howe was the minister of the government responsible for trade and commerce, the man whose policies were responsible for the export of Canada's surplus grain. Trade policy is the responsibility of government, but under the previous administration the farmer was left to bear the burden of the problems created by lack of trade. The article to which I referred as an illustration of the previous government's failure to recognize the position of agriculture reads in part as follows:
A bronzed farmer rushed into the Carman memorial hall as Mr. Howe was leaving and thrust a piece of paper into his hand which purported to show that it cost 76 cents a bushel to grow oats. "Why'd you cut the price from 60 to 55 cents?" demanded the farmer. Mr. Howe asked him where he got the figure. The farmer said that it was from "statistics".
The reply of the then minister of trade and commerce revealed the attitude of the previous government, which was the reason for its failure and collapse, the reason it deserved to be defeated. What did the minister reply? As reported in this article the minister said:
"You look pretty well fed." said the trade minister, patting the farmer on the stomach with the back of his hand.
There could not have been a clearer presentation of what agriculture really requires than the words of this young farmer, who asked a straightforward, simple and logical question of the minister of the former government who was responsible for Canada's trade policies. It was just as simple as this. The young farmer came forward and in effect said, "These are my costs of production according to your own bureau of statistics, and this is the selling price of my product according to the policy under which you sell my goods. I am skinning my costs down to the very bone. I have done my job in producing food for the hungry world. Your policies of trade have affected the markets where I sell my grain. Now, what are you going to do about it?" The reply was, "You look pretty well fed."
The former government's Agricultural Prices Support Act failed to recognize the principle of parity. The act did not contain this principle, and the former government failed to accept this principle. The Conservative government has now brought forward Bill No. 237, and our quarrel with it is that it, too, fails to accept, recognize or embody the principle of parity.
The former government would place no guarantee on the farmer's costs in its legislation. Under the act it did support prices on a few commodities such as hogs, which were supported at 23 cents in Toronto which
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization meant a support of approximately 21 cents in Winnipeg and 19 cents to farmers in Saskatchewan. These supports were at disastrous levels. Egg prices were guaranteed to packing plants, without any protection to the farmer. It is little wonder that agriculture found itself in such desperate straits and suffered a gradual decline, while the food processing and packing industries reaped tremendous dividends. The present bill fails in exactly the same way. Can it be that this government has already lost touch with the actual every-day problems of the farmer?

Well, it stated in this house that it was. Agriculture today requires legislation which will guarantee the farmer relief from the cost-price squeeze. It is the government and not the producer that is responsible for the costs of production. When the previous government, supported by the Conservative party at that time, removed price controls and allowed costs to skyrocket it condemned agriculture to its present plight. The farmer is caught in a cost-price squeeze from which he cannot extract himself, and he now relies on the present government to help him out. He looks to this government for this assistance because this government promised him that help.
Members of the present government from the Prime Minister down talked about parity in this house when they were in opposition. They supported and moved resolutions in this house while in opposition which would guarantee the farmer parity. Conservative candidates during the campaign went about the country advocating a program designed to assist agriculture. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources had the nerve yesterday to quote in this house some of the planks of the Conservative platform having to do with agriculture, as recorded at page 3621 of Hansard of yesterday's date. I will read one or two of these platform planks:
1. The Progressive Conservative party recognizes the vital place of agriculture in our national economy, stands pledged to assure the maximum stability of income to Canadian farmers.
It guarantees nothing. These are hollow promises, empty, meaningless words.
No. 2 reads:
Our party pledges itself, when returned to power, to take action to improve the condition of agriculture so that our farm people will re-establish their rightful position in our economy, so basic to, our whole national welfare.
Splendid; now do it. Then we come to No. 3r
A Progressive Conservative government wilt maintain a flexible price support program to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers, based: on fair price-cost relationship.

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
That is where this government has failed, because it is failing to ensure parity. It does not mention the word "parity" in this bill. It does not mention a fair price-cost relationship in the bill. It fails to give the guarantee which it promised. We will accept this bill when those guarantees are written into it. We will not accept this bill until they are written into it, until there are some guarantees written into it such as the Conservative party stated in the program they presented to the Canadian people, such as the people expected when they voted this government into power.
This government was elected on June 10 and hope rose in the hearts of many people. Then a resolution appeared on the order paper shortly after October 14. Speaking to that resolution the Minister of Agriculture himself used these words, as recorded at page 2187 of Hansard of December 11. In dealing with what the farmer wants he said:
First, he wants prices for his products which will cover his cost of production and leave him enough to live on-
Exactly.
-and second, he desires a sense of security in his price structure, the removal of his long-time fear that prices will fall away to nothing while his crop is growing or his livestock developing to market size.
Then why in Heaven's name don't you do it?

I am referring to the bill now before us, Bill No. 237, with the amendments. The minister says the bill will do this. Why did he not put some guarantees in it; why did he not put the security in it that he says is here? That is all the farmer is asking for. All the farmer is asking for is exactly what the minister said, but he will not put them in the bill. They are not in the bill. It is exactly a sense of security that is required. Then the minister said, as recorded at page 2189 of Hansard:
I think this legislation will do everything we promised we would do so far as our campaign pledges are concerned.
 *
Here is the bill. It was brought in on December 14. I think it should be called a pill rather than a bill. Certainly the minister was so ashamed of it that he made three amendments shortly after, but those amendments do absolutely nothing basic with regard to the guarantees which are necessary, and it is the guarantees that we are talking about. It is all right to talk about stabilization boards which may do this and that, and about advisory committees which may do this and that under certain regulations by order in council; but there is nothing in the bill which says this is where prices must stay; below this range prices will not be allowed to fall and those prices will be, as the minister states in his own words, such as "will cover his cost of production and leave him enough to live on". When the minister puts this in his bill we will be glad to accept it.
We have asked him to send this bill to the agriculture committee of the house. Let the agriculture committee deal with it. Since December 12 this bill could have gone to that committee. It could have been passed earlier in the session, the committee could have been dealing with it and the minister could have received some of those recommendations from farmers and farm organizations across the country. But he came down with a bill which is a mere will o' the wisp, and nothing substantial has been done.
The bill has aroused opposition from every quarter of organized agriculture, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the provincial farm unions, the western wheat pools and others. This is what the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had to say about it after they received a copy of the bill in the amended form:
The formula in the new bill provides for a moving average of recent prices, with no necessary relation to costs.
That is what we need; that is what we are asking for. I continue:
The government says the use of a parity formula would lead to rigid price supports. The C.F.A. does not accept this: it grants that flexibility must be allowed in actually setting supports but claims that without a parity formula as a guide the economic position of the farmer becomes a constant matter of controversy.
We are going to have recommendations by stabilization boards, recommendations to cabinet, with no instructions to carry them out. There is no assurance that they will be carried out, and we are constantly going to have confusion. There will be requests for something to be done, but the farmer will be left in uncertainty and he cannot help but be left in confusion. Why not place something in the bill which relates the price of his commodity to his costs of production? If that was placed

in the bill we might have something. The federation's statement goes on to say:
This makes much more difficult constructive negotiation of price supports and useful discussion of measures needed to meet the farmers' problem.
The formula which is mentioned in this amended bill is based on the average wholesale market price for the past 10 years, and bears absolutely no relationship to the farmer's parity position.
It should be pointed out to everyone that if you follow the basic prices established by this formula they automatically continue to decline. Just so long as there is a trend toward lower farm prices, prices of farm commodities are going to decline. As long as there is a trend toward lower prices those lower guaranteed prices will persist, even though farm costs may continue to increase to higher and still higher levels, because in the bill as it stands at the present time there is no proper meshing of these two things together so the farmer himself can arrive at a stable price which would allow him to plan his production in advance and put himself in a position where he can possibly meet the serious situation which he is now facing.
This bill lacks definite assurances and guarantees which the government said in its program the farmers would have; definite assurances and guarantees which the farm organizations have asked for; definite assurances that the farm organizations have asked for in their representations to the government on this bill. Under this bill the economic position of the farmer could even deteriorate; it all depends on the whim of the government and their own regulations. The bill lacks guarantees; it lacks assurances.
It is because the bill provides no stability that we are protesting it so vigorously at this time. Those who sent us here sent us to ask for a square deal for agriculture, to ask that the family farm might be saved as the cornerstone of our economy. Under this legislation there is no assurance whatsoever that the family farm will not disappear, to be replaced by the large factory farm or the contract farm, as has happened in many countries and is happening in some parts even here in Canada.
The large packing house operators, the rich processing industries, will hire the farmer and his family to produce commodities for them at contract rates. The farmers will take all the risks and the processors will reap the profits because of a system of support prices guaranteeing floor prices in the storage plant, with rider clauses to guarantee the processor floor prices in storage and the costs of storage.
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
What this bill will have to do before we will support it is provide guarantees as to the prices the farmer receives, the prices in the hands of the producer, in the hands of the man who does the work and takes the risks. We believe this is a last ditch fight for hundreds of thousands of family farms across Canada. It is a fight to obtain some anchor of security for one of the most important industries in our economy. Instead of an anchor of security the minister has given us a balloon which he launched into the air to see how the wind was blowing.
This bill has no guarantees and it leaves the farmer without any assurance, even though he is engaged in the hazardous occupation of growing food for a hungry world. In that fine occupation, because of circumstances completely beyond his control, he has reached the verge of bankruptcy. Just as surely as the wage earner needs a minimum wage in these days of high costs of living, so the farmer must have support prices based on his production costs. The disposal of surplus products is surely the duty of the government. With the situation existing in the world today the farmer should not be compelled to carry an extra load on his already breaking back. The family farm must not be allowed to be sacrificed by a government which promised to save it. The only policy which can save it is a policy having as its foundation the principle of parity.
The bill ignores the principle of parity completely, and for that reason it must be condemned completely. We intend to continue to condemn it and to do our utmost to change it in order to make it into a piece of legislation that will at last place some foundation under this important industry. Yesterday the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources had the unmitigated gall to imply that the bill brought security and peace of mind to the long-harassed farmers of Canada, and those of western Canada particularly. What a farce. What complete misrepresentation of a bill which has within it no guarantees of security. How can a producer possibly have peace of mind if he has to operate under legislation which has no guarantees in it at all?
We shall continue to fight the battle with every means at our disposal until we are able to establish a sound foundation for security in the bill. There must be recognition of the right of the farmer to his costs of production and enough money on which to live. That is all he is asking. The bill as it stands today can be termed nothing but a callous betrayal of people who on June 10 last were given some glimmer of hope that if the Conservatives were elected to office they would

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization place a proper foundation under agriculture. The bill is a complete denial of the promise and betrayal of that hope. The people of Canada should and will reject the bill in its present form, and they will reject everyone who supports it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as this is the first time I have spoken in the house I beg your indulgence for the remarks I am about to make. At this late stage in the session it may be redundant to congratulate you upon your election to office. However, I should like to say that having observed your conduct in the house since the beginning of the session and the good humoured way in which you have handled some of the more sensitive situations which have arisen, I feel that the confidence placed in you by hon. members has long since been justified.
To all hon. members, and more particularly to those who are veteran members, I wish to express my appreciation for the cordial and friendly attitude which has been displayed by them to a new member.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I take great pride in paying tribute to my leader the Prime Minister, who I am satisfied will eventually be acclaimed and acknowledged as the greatest prime minister this country has ever had.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in order to give the house some idea of the importance of agriculture in my riding, I should like to point out that farming has been carried on in Northumberland since the latter part of the fourteenth century. The early pioneers were composed of people from the British Isles and the United States, retired members of military units of that day. These people cleared and worked the land, and in many cases their descendants still occupy the original farms created many years ago. As a result of their efforts places like Cobourg, Campbellford, Brighton, Colborne and Hastings sprang up, as well as many other smaller communities.
At one time wheat was the main product of my riding. Every year hundreds of wagonloads of grain were loaded into sailing 
vessels at the numerous ports that dotted the lake front along lake Ontario. Even at that time wheat was commanding a price as high as $1.00 a bushel. The farmers of Northumberland had an outstanding reputation for the wheat they grew. In 1832 the first thresher used in Upper Canada was brought into Northumberland. In 1843 the first Hussey reaper in Upper Canada was used near Cobourg, and in 1847 the first McCormick reaper in Upper Canada was also used near Cobourg.
There are agricultural organizations in my riding which have been in existence for over 100 years. In 1952 the Brighton agricultural society celebrated the one hundredth anniversary of the Brighton fall fair. The Seymour and Percy agricultural societies have likewise marked the one hundredth anniversaries of the Campbellford and Wark-worth fall fairs. The Roseneath fall fair is one of the finest of its kind in eastern Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, I think the foregoing should serve to illustrate the background of my riding as an agricultural community, and it is still essentially an agricultural community. Northumberland is an area of mixed farming, made up of small or family type farms. Vegetables are grown as a cash crop and processed by the local canning factories. There are milk producers, beef producers, hog producers, poultry and egg producers. There are commercial dairies and cheese factories. In spite of any claim that might be made by any other hon. member on behalf of his riding, the finest McIntosh and Northern Spy apples in the world are grown by the apple growers of Northumberland. Honey producers and potato growers are also found within the limits of my riding, and in recent years a considerable number of tobacco growers have become established.
Although agriculture is not the only industry of importance in Northumberland, I consider it to be the most important industry, and have therefore chosen to speak for the first time in the house on this agricultural stabilization bill. In doing so I am not holding myself out as an expert on the subject, but only as a member endeavouring to represent his constituents. I want to address my remarks particularly to hon. members who do not represent rural ridings and who consequently may not be aware of the necessity for legislation of this kind. Almost every member who has participated in this debate has pointed out the depressed state into which agriculture has fallen over the last few years. The situation in my riding is no exception. The prices received for agricultural products

have not increased in proportion to the cost of equipment which farmers require to carry on their activities.
It is not necessary to quote figures. They have been quoted by other speakers, and they are also a matter of record. As a result of those conditions farmers in many cases are producing at a loss. There is absolutely no incentive for the younger people to stay on the farms, and they are leaving in large numbers. Many farmers in my riding actually find it necessary to work off the farm in order to supplement their income. This story has been repeated again and again in this house and elsewhere, but it bears repetition because it reflects a serious situation.
In my opinion the question we have to decide is whether or not it is to our benefit to maintain agriculture as a national industry. If we do not consider agriculture worth while to maintain, eventually we will be placed in the position of having to rely on someone else to feed us, and in the event of a third world war we would have to accept whatever hand-outs we could get from other countries. This whole question affects our survival as a nation. If on the other hand we do consider that agriculture should be maintained, then we must be prepared to support and stabilize it, and this bill is designed to do just that.
There are other good reasons, Mr. Speaker, for supporting agriculture as an industry. During world war II, when through force of circumstances farmers were placed in a good bargaining position, ceiling prices were put on farm products. This measure was accepted by farmers as necessary and for the general welfare of the nation. Having asked the farmers to assume that regulation, we should now be prepared to give them the corresponding privilege of supporting and stabilizing farm prices with funds from the public treasury.
Another point which should be mentioned is the effect of the status of agriculture on the economy as a whole. A great deal of concern has been expressed about unemployment since this* session began, and various suggestions have been made as to how the problem could be best overcome. The farmer constitutes a large proportion of the purchasing power of this country, and if farmers were put in the position where they could operate at a profit it would be a boost to the entire economy, not only as a result of the extra money that would be in circulation but as a result of the many jobs that would be opened when farmers no longer found it necessary to work off the farm to make a living.
I should like now to deal briefly with the bill itself. I consider that the speaker who
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization immediately preceded me made one of the more rational and less impassioned speeches to be made by any member of his group, although it still did not convince me that this bill is not going to do the job for agriculture that we want done.
This bill represents the first attempt by any government to introduce long-term legislation of a comprehensive nature to put agriculture in Canada on a sound basis. Its objective is to give some stability to farm prices and to raise farm incomes to the level where farming can be carried on at a profit instead of at a loss. In this respect I am pleased to support it, because I think it represents a definite step in the right direction. As the minister pointed out, it is not a panacea or cure-all for agriculture, but it is a sincere attempt to put a floor under agriculture and to raise it to a proper level.
The bill introduces entirely new concepts as far as Canadian agricultural price support legislation is concerned. The features of guaranteed forward pricing and a statutory permanent floor price are progressive and forward-looking measures. To my mind, so many members of the opposition have been so keen to criticize the bill that they have missed entirely the significance of these new features which are so far-reaching in their implications.
I feel that the farmers of my riding consider that this bill is a step in the right direction and would wish me to support it. As far as the amendment to refer the bill to the agriculture committee is concerned, I think such a move would only serve to delay its passage indefinitely and would thereby deprive the farmers of its benefits. I therefore cannot support such an amendment.
In speaking on this bill at the present stage the right hon. member for Melville, the former minister of agriculture, made an attempt which was far short of convincing to compare this bill with the present Agricultural Prices Support Act. Mr. Speaker, one might just as well attempt to compare an old flivver with a new car. There may be some slight similarity, but the new model has many modern and up to date features which the old one has not. The present act was originally enacted to assist the farmers in the transition from war to peace whenever that should be. It was at best only designed as a temporary measure, and making it permanent did not change its nature. It contains no guarantees whatsoever. Supports can be put in and taken off at random, and the farmer never knows where he is.
The record of performance of the present act is contained between the covers of the
3684	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization blue book entitled "The Agricultural Prices Support Board-Annual Report to the Minister of Agriculture for the Year 195657". It has supported ten products since 1946 at a cost to the national treasury of $24 million in regular price supports. Apart from the record outlined in the report, if the act had been of any value agriculture would not now be in its present state.
I should now like to deal briefly with some of the statements made by the right hon. member for Melville in discussing the act and the bill. He says the act is more flexible. In that contention he may be correct but, by the same token, the act has no stability. The bill has both, and both are important. If I were a farmer I would be most anxious to know that the price of a product I was about to produce would not drop out of sight during the long period of production. If I knew there was a minimum fixed amount beyond which the price could not drop during that period, I could commence production with a much greater sense of security and confidence. If this minimum amount was set at a realistic figure and taking into consideration my probable cost of production, I would feel that much more secure.
That is stability, and that is the purpose of this bill. That is why one of the most important features of this bill is that of advance price supports. The formula in the bill also ensures that there will be some relationship between price supports set for various products, so that a balanced production may be maintained.
The right hon. member also mentioned deficiency payments. I would point out that this bill also contains provision for deficiency payments where necessary. He further mentioned that the act has a three-year basis which is fundamental to that legislation. The three years are 1943, 1944 and 1945, and he says, "We took that basis because farmers were fairly well satisfied at the time". The act was passed in 1944, at which time he could not possibly have known that the farmers were satisfied in 1945. Hence the only conclusion that can be drawn is that he was assuming that farmers would be fairly well satisfied in 1945.
Another matter mentioned by the right hon. member for Melville was the committee appointed under the act. The right hon. member said he never at any time asked the present committee to advise on specific things. My reaction is that a committee without a specific job will accomplish nothing; and as far as coming to the minister is concerned, any farm organization should be at leisure to come to the minister on any mutually
[Mr. Thompson (Northumberland) .1

satisfactory date to discuss anything it wishes. Such being the case, what necessity is there for a committee at all unless it has a specific job to do? The advisory committee contemplated by the bill has a specific job to do, and it will therefore be done.
I am not going to pursue any further the attempt made by the right hon. member to compare the act and the bill. Suffice it to say that I consider that his arguments with regard to flexibility, the basis of setting support prices, stabilization, the advisory committee, the functioning of the present act and also his justification for supporting the bill do not stand up under the slightest examination.
I should like to commend the present Minister of Agriculture for the amount of effort he has put into preparing this bill. I think the amendments he proposes to make, after having received the representations and suggestions of various farm organizations, as well as the suggestions of the members of this house, indicate a sincere desire on his part to introduce legislation of real benefit to the farmers of this country. It has been pointed out previously that price supports alone will not provide the whole answer to the agricultural problem. There are many aspects to the problem. The fruit and vegetable growers say it will be of little or no benefit to them, although they are not criticizing it when they say that. What they require is more protection from imports so they can have the benefit of our own markets.
I was surprised at the remarks made by the present Leader of the Opposition when he was discussing the matter of trade earlier this session. He suggested that if we wanted to get along with our big neighbour to the south, tradewise, we would have to play ball. His idea of playing ball apparently is to allow a United States tariff twice as high as our Canadian tariff on the same agricultural product. It is a fact that this condition now exists and has existed; and surely if there is to be any variation in tariff between the two countries on the same product it should be the other way around. He also criticized the Prime Minister for protesting out loud against the trade policies of the United States. I wonder how he justifies this criticism having regard to his own agricultural policy unveiled last week.
During the course of the debate yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West, whom I consider to be a very fine gentleman, referred to a meeting which had taken place in my riding during the Christmas recess. I am satisfied to let the hon. member derive whatever little comfort he can derive from having read the report of that

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
meeting. I would, however, like to say that the report he read was not at all accurate. The meeting was not nearly as large as he made it out to be. It was only a meeting attended by a few members of the executive of the local farm union. I might also say that since the meeting I have heard from several people who attended, saying they did not agree with what went on at the meeting.
I feel that I know the people in my riding and they are reasonable people, people of sober reflection. Having had the opportunity to look at this bill and consider it at length, I am satisfied that they are ready to go along with it and support it. That is much more than can be said of the members of the C.C.F. group.
I do not know whether I should take exception to a remark made by the hon. member when he referred to the quickness with which the people of my riding move. From my own observations since I have been in this house I think the people in my riding move just as quickly as people anywhere else. During this session I have gathered that the members of that group subscribe to the proposition that the more voluble you are and the more quickly you speak, the more intelligent you therefore are. In other words volubility and quickness of speech is to them a mark of intelligence, and conversely slowness of speech is a mark of ignorance. This may serve to justify all the talking they have been doing since the beginning of the session, but I do not think it necessarily proves that the proposition is correct.

In concluding my remarks I would say that I am pleased to hear that the minister intends to keep an eye on the operation of the legislation to make sure that at all times the benefit of the support prices is passed on to the producers, and also that the farm organizations are to be consulted as to whom they may wish to represent them on the advisory committee. speechtext:
There are one or two things I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, which are within the purview of this bill now before the house. I do so with the knowledge that the farming population of my county and of the province in which I live is directly concerned with any measure respecting the welfare of the agricultural industry.
This bill is intended to stabilize the prices of agricultural products. The farmers in my own area are particularly engaged in the dairy and livestock branches of the industry, and as such have already had an opportunity of appreciating the benefits of price supports on pork and butter as provided by the prices support act. They realize it is mainly through this legislation that they have been able to remain in the industry, and I therefore listened with concern to the Minister of Agriculture use the example of the price of butter to illustrate how this proposed measure would function. His statement that under this new act the minimum price set on butter would now be 48 cents per pound did not carry too cheerful a note to the ears of those interested in this matter.
I am prepared to admit that it is not the intention of the government to allow the price of' this commodity to fall to that level, at least so far as they are directly concerned. However, as was so clearly stated by the former minister of agriculture, the right hon. member for Melville, once a price is set by law trade tends to gravitate toward that price, and it would be very unfortunate indeed if the price on butter were to be thus affected.
3686	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
There is one other aspect of the situation to which I should like to draw the attention of this house. I refer to pulpwood as a farm product. This has been mentioned [DOT] already during the course of the present debate, and I am inclined to agree with those who make the claim that pulpwood should fall within the scope of the proposed bill. This might appear as a novelty, having regard to the economy of western agriculture, but it is none the less a matter of vital importance particularly in the economy of the maritime agricultural industry.
I know that farmers in my riding-and this situation applies to most sections of New Brunswick-depend upon revenue derived from farm wood lots as an essential part of their annual revenue. I am also well aware that many farmers are hard pressed today on account of the stalemate in the pulpwood industry. Therefore the situation in this respect could very well be compared with the situation of the western farmer unable to sell his wheat. I would therefore welcome any action on the part of the government which would have the effect of assisting farm pulpwood producers under this bill.
I believe we cannot overemphasize the necessity of taking a very close look at the present state of the agricultural economy, more particularly with respect to the economy of the so-called subsistence farmer.
This is now indicating the effects of a deep, broad evolution. Many small farms have had to be abandoned, while their owners were forced to seek employment in the labour field for the subsistence of their family. It appears to me to be an appalling situation to have former farm owners now on the labour market looking for work and depending upon unemployment insurance for their subsistence, while their farm lots are idle and unproductive.
This is more than just such a bad situation. It is a challenge to the administrative powers of the country. It is only fair to say that an economy which permits people who are unable to find work in the labour field to face the dread of hunger while these same people are the owners of good, fertile farm lots, irrespective of their size, is a situation not a credit to our economic system. A solution should be found under which a farm owner at least would not be haunted with the fear of want, let alone be denied the opportunity of making any financial profits.
The bill now before this house remains to be proven, and I want to warn the present government that in view of its electoral promises it will be held highly responsible by the farm people of this country if the results achieved by this bill do not provide


a satisfactory solution to the present agricultural situation. If this government feels in its own mind that it can give the assurance that this bill will provide this solution, then I am prepared to support it, in lieu of a more concrete definite and precise measure, which I would have liked to see.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the remarks of previous speakers from all sides of the house with reference to this bill and to the opinions expressed on it by various farm organizations and by our farmers at home in Prince Edward Island. The constituency of Kings, which I have the honour to represent, is comprised mainly of farmers and fishermen, much the same as the other two counties in my native province.
I make no pretense of being a farmer, even though I grow a few acres of potatoes each year, but ever since the war, when I began doing business with the farmers as a general merchant and a shipper of produce, I have been acutely conscious of their difficulties. Their problems have been my problems. And as they have discussed them with me daily, I can assure hon. members from close personal knowledge and observation that many of our farmers have been forced to undergo severe hardships in the past few years.
The position of the farmer has become more and more untenable, so that farms are being abandoned at an alarming rate. In 1911 the number of farms in operation in our province was 14,163. Over the next 30 years the number dropped to 12,230. In the next 10 years the number dropped to 10,137, and we all know the number has taken a further serious drop since 1951. In our province there has been very little amalgamation of farms into larger units, and not much corporate farming. The crux of our problem is that farm prices have just not kept up with the costs of production, and farmers have been forced out of the industry for financial reasons and young men have been unable to take up farming.
Our province has no land settlement policy, and the assistance provided by the Farm Loan Board leaves much to be desired under the present regulations. I do not intend to go into the farming problems of our area in detail, as that would take too long a time, other than to affirm that conditions are not good in the farming industry in the province of Prince Edward Island. Many of the farmers are not cultivating their farms, only living on them. Young men are shying away from going into farming, and the industry generally has become much weaker. More than anything else the farmer in our province wants stability in his industry. Along with

the other primary producer, the fisherman, he sutlers from instability of crop return and price income as no other worth-while industry does in this country.
Our party has promised that in order to overcome this problem there should be a flexible price support program. Although the farmer has suffered unjustly for the past number of years he is a responsible individual in every way, and probably gives more thought to national problems than any other class of citizen. He is not asking for support prices that will produce large surpluses, which will have to be given away, or worse still, destroyed, to relieve a glut on the market.
We all know what happened in the United States, and we should not be irresponsible enough to follow a program such as theirs. According to a recent United States Department of Agriculture Press Release for the fiscal year 1957 the cost of price support was $3.3 billion. There are a total of 4.8 million farms in the United States. Most price supports go to 1.3 million of them on large scale farms, the owners of which receive an average of $2,000 per farm. The other 3.7 million of the small farms received an average of slightly more than $100 per farm. In plain words the plan of our neighbours to the south tended to make the rich richer, and was of very little help to the small farmer.
We are all aware, too, of the great difficulty and embarrassment that surpluses produced under this plan have caused in world markets. We in Canada have directly felt the effects of United States give-away programs resulting from their agricultural policy. They are now faced with the prospect of further reducing their percentage of parity. Let us benefit from their errors and ensure that we do not get into the same unhappy position as the government of that country. This bill provides the flexibility that is needed in such legislation-which is reasonable and fair to all.
It is necessary at this point, Mr. Speaker, that there be a clear understanding of the problem of prices from the viewpoint of the consumer as well as from that of the producer. Some consumers have no objection to increased prices for various household commodities, automobiles, etc., yet object to any increases in food prices. There is a certain element of unfairness in this attitude, in that the prices of the former commodities have risen greatly whereas the prices of many agricultural products have risen little or not at all. It is not necessary to point out again that there has been a sharp increase in the cost of everything the farmer must buy such as machinery, automobiles and household effects. I feel strongly that a definite campaign
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization should be instituted to educate the consumer to understand the position of the producer and to appreciate that the primary producer should be entitled to a fair return for his labour and his investment, which is a big item today; and that he should be entitled to a fair share of the national income.
One feature of this bill which I feel deserves special commendation is the consideration of pulpwood on the farm as a product within the scope of the proposed legislation. This is a branch of farming which has produced considerable income for our farmers, and is particularly valuable in supplementing income during the winter months. Any assistance, even to a limited extent, would be greatly appreciated by our farmers.
One coming from Prince Edward Island could not speak of agriculture without mentioning the important place of potato growing in that industry. Without fear of contradiction, Mr. Speaker, I can say it is well known that we grow the best potatoes in the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although we have already heard quite a number of members on this subject, still in a sense it is with a bit of reluctance that one gets up to speak on this bill. There is no doubt that the minister and the government mean well; there is no doubt that they want to help the farmers just as much as any other members in this house; but, of course, they want to do it in their own way.
To get up at this time and state that one is not in favour of this bill as it stands now; or if one gets up and criticizes this bill, even if it is constructive criticism, even if the criticism is made with the full intention of trying to make a sincere contribution to agriculture, might be misinterpreted in some quarters as a gesture of opposition to the cause of agriculture and the betterment of the farmer's position across the country.
Indeed, already I can almost see persons getting up either in this house or in other places and saying the Liberals are opposed to the welfare of the farmers and are not interested in solving the problems that exist. These persons will point to the fact that some Liberals rose in their places in the house and spoke against this bill, and they will say, "You see, I told you; this bill was meant to help agriculture. This man got up and spoke against this bill, so he is against agriculture." I can already hear this oversimplified argument, which is entirely false and misleading; yet it will be laid on like a gramaphone record in all the constituencies across the country.
This sort of disruptive argument by innuendo has already been practised in this house, when an hon. member said, "It should be remembered that there is no farm member from Manitoba representing the Liberal party." I had to rise on that occasion, Mr. Speaker, and state quite clearly that the constituency of St. Boniface is a semi-rural and semi-urban constituency, and that the electors of St. Boniface know very well that I am keenly interested in agriculture. If I had left the remark of my hon. friend unanswered the impression would have been created that he was right and that there were no Liberals in Manitoba interested in agriculture. He thought I was not in this house, or he does not know St. Boniface. The moral of the story is, of course, that when you do not know you do not say.
This point having been straightened out, there remains unfortunately the whispering campaign and the intensive propaganda circulated in the last election campaign which


went around creating the impression that the Liberals were not interested in the problems of the farmers. The big mistake made by the Liberals at that time was to let the propaganda float around with insufficient information and correction. The Liberal party has always been interested in agriculture and it still is. One has only to read the proceedings of the last Liberal convention to realize that. One has only to recall the resolutions brought in by the delegation from Manitoba to know that we lead the way in the field of agriculture.
I have observed with great interest the approach of the minister to the problems of agriculture and how he finally emerged with the present concoction which, to my way of thinking, does not give us anything better than the act it proposes to repeal and be substituted for. I am speaking, of course, of the present Agricultural Prices Support Act, which has been in force for some time.
I know, and I stated in the house during the debate on the throne speech, that the problem of agriculture is not new to Canada. It has been with us for many years, and it is so great that it will remain with us for a good number of years. It cannot be solved in one day. As a matter of fact there are very few solutions that can be of a permanent nature because of the economics of the problem.
Therefore I am surprised that the minister seems to take the attitude that he will almost solve the problems in one bill. Oh, I know that lately he backtracked and said that this was no panacea; that one bill would not solve all the problems, but action speaks louder than words. What is the minister doing?
The minister was asked on December 14 by the hon. member for Assiniboia whether he would not give the house the assurance that the bill would be referred to the agriculture committee so it could be studied in all its details. The minister replied that he could not give the assurance, and I quote from page 2393 of Hansard:
If what the hon. member proposes was done this bill would not be through for months.
The minister then added:
In other words, if the bill were sent to the agricultural committee and we had there a full discussion of various types of what support policies might be put into effect and their advantages and disadvantages and so forth, it would certainly take weeks, and I am sure it would take months. The total effect would be that the bill itself would not be through and it would not be possible to put it into effect and the farmers of this country would not get the benefits of it.
The minister felt on December 14-perhaps he does not feel that way any more-that he had discovered the panacea to solve the problems of the farmers. Having in mind his feelings toward this bill I am sure some partisans

will take advantage of the simple fact that I have risen and told the minister that I am not in agreement with him. As a matter of fact it would appear that in some quarters some people think the opposition is strictly a voting machine, even if it appears that what an hon. member is saying is constructive criticism, and that is exactly my approach to this bill, criticism of a constructive nature.
I have had occasion to compare the present bill with the present legislation, and I cannot say at this stage that it gives us very much. Of course some amendments have now been made, but it was with great difficulty that we finally obtained copies of the amendments.
You will all recall what happened in December. The minister indicated that there were amendments to be made, and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested that the bill be withdrawn, reprinted and presented to the house again. 1 suggested at that time that we should at least have copies of the amendments in order that they could be properly studied.
There was quite an argument. At first the minister was lukewarm to that suggestion. Then he suggested that perhaps the amendments were not that substantial. He was supported by two of his colleagues in the cabinet, who intimated that the amendments were not substantial. This leads me to make two points. First, if they were not substan-r tial amendments then why is it that one of them is actually the preamble to the bill? Everybody knows that the preamble to a bill outlines the principles of the bill. Therefore in effect the minister was admitting at that time, as did two of his colleagues, that the principles of the bill were not substantial. Try to defeat the logic of that argument.
Something else happened on that occasion which really surprised me. The Acting Prime Minister covered up the procedure adopted by the Minister of Agriculture by saying that he was merely following the practice of previous governments. I should like to know if an intelligent man can be asked to make an intelligent study and an intelligent decision regarding matters and facts of which he has no knowledge or only limited knowledge. It is a fair presumption that all members of the house are intelligent, whether they are backbenchers or not, and obviously a member of the house should have the text of any legislation upon which he is being asked to vote.
Two wrongs do not make a right. If any practice is basically wrong I cannot see why it should be adhered to whether it has been in operation for one year or 100 years; and
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization to hide behind such a weak argument is indeed the most extravagant display and confession of one's own weakness. I might add, Mr. Speaker, and in this I imagine I am voicing the feelings of most members of the house, that I have not been elected by the electors of St. Boniface to become a rubber stamp for the decisions that might arise out of the deliberations of a selected very few.
As others have said in the house, the bill represents some progress in price support legislation. Price guarantees are to be in effect at all times on key commodities. Price supports will be reviewed annually and established on key commodities twelve months in advance. We find also that there is provision for a larger revolving fund. A minimum guaranteed floor is also a desirable feature. There is certainly in the bill a stab in the right direction, and I am sure it is the intention of the minister that his purposes should always be aimed in the right direction.
I venture to say there is still a lot that could be done to make this a better bill. This would obviously take time, but there is no rush about the bill. We could go on for a few months with what we already have on the statute books. What I say is, could we not try to make it better? This bill, while it recognizes certain principles which might very well be in the interests of the farmers, will not in the next few months give more to the farmers in actual cash than what the farmers can get under the present legislation. Of course after the bill is in effect the board directed by the minister or the governor in council possibly could try to play Santa Claus at some time immediately prior to the next general election and try to get the full credit for it. But if anybody is to play Santa Claus with the taxpayers' money it is for this house to do so, not for the board, the minister or the government.
I would have thought that after the question of the hon. member for Assiniboia on December 14 the minister would have given a better reply to his further question of December 17, when he asked if the minister was prepared to reverse his decision and have the bill referred to the committee on agriculture. I would venture to say that when the minister took office he did not know very much more about agriculture than most lawyers know, but he has approached the problem in commendable ways which appear sound and logical. He is earnest and means well.
Perhaps, however, the minister should accept a little more advice. It appears that somehow at a certain stage he felt that he had solved the problem, and then produced this bill. Now it has become apparent that
3690	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization although he had gone correctly part of the way, there was and there still is quite a bit to do. Many are begging him to have the bill referred to the agriculture committee, but he says there is no time. I guess there is no time now, but there was time on December 14.
I would ask him what is the rush. Of course the problems of agriculture are urgent. There is need to help the farmers, and this as soon as possible; but it is not by simply producing a bill and calling it the agricultural stabilization act or an act to provide for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities that the problems of the farmers will necessarily be solved. The essence of the bill is what is important, not the intention of the minister. The intention of the minister is no criterion of what is right or wrong. Many people have had good intentions, yet the ways in which they tried to implement them turned out to be insufficient, and the desired results were not achieved.
We have passed a number of bills which were of an emergency nature. The legislation respecting cash advances on grain is a perfect example. That was stop-gap legislation. It was strictly an emergency measure, and this opinion has been confirmed by hundreds of farmers to whom I have spoken and with whom I have corresponded since that legislation was passed. But there is not the same urgency, the same immediate need, having regard particularly to the fact that the present bill does not cure the need that it pretends to want to cure. We have had quite an amount of legislation at this session which is strictly a hand-out prior to the next general election, but surely the government does not expect that this bill will help the farming population sufficiently; and I would suggest that upon reflection further study is necessary.
I understand that if the bill were referred to the committee on agriculture we would then have the advantage of hearing evidence from farm organizations. We would have the privilege of hearing the experts. I feel quite sure, in spite of the fact there are in the house a great number of members, including the minister, who are more and more conversant with the problem of agriculture, that we would gain immensely in dealing with agricultural problems generally by having the benefit of hearing more from the farmers of all parts of Canada. The minister, while relenting the other day, admitted that his bill was no cure-all. I agree entirely. But what about a better prescription, well analysed and better prepared, before forcing it upon the patient?
There is opposition to the bill. Many meetings have been held by farm organizations


in western Canada, particularly in Manitoba and more particularly in my own constituency during the Christmas recess. I was confronted at that time with great opposition from the farmers regarding this bill and I feel it is my duty to say so in the house. Furthermore, I have here a letter which I have received. I propose to give the full text, its origin and everything. It was written to me by a man who is a district director of the Manitoba farmers' union, Mr. Neil Simon-sen. He writes to me from Sanford, Manitoba, under date of December 15, 1957.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make just a few more observations. I am not prepared to go as far as some members of the C.C.F. party want to go. I actually believe, quite'sincerely, that they exaggerate. I feel quite certain that if they ever felt there was a possibility, as we on this side of the house do, that some day they would form a government, they would never be as extravagant as they are. We know quite well that soon or later we will be on the other side of the house and we feel, therefore, we should adopt a responsible attitude towards farm problems.
Then, I should like to say a word with regard to the amendment which, if I recall correctly, is to the effect that this matter be referred to the agriculture committee. I was in favour of this amendment in December. However, there have been statements made that perhaps in 10 days, or a short time thereafter, the session will be completed and this makes it impossible to have the bill referred to the agriculture committee. I am in favour of the principle of the amendment however, and so far as this particular amendment is concerned I simply must register the fact that I shall have to abstain from voting. I cannot vote against a principle in which I

believe, and on the other hand I cannot vote in favour of something I believe to be impractical.
In so far as the bill itself is concerned, after everything I have said today which stems from the studies I have made, and also as a result of the instructions and representations I have received from not only my own constituency but from all over the province of Manitoba, I must state that I cannot vote in favour of this bill.
