Mr. Speaker, as a representative from a large rural constituency, I am glad to take part in the debate on second reading of this agricultural stabilization bill. I do so in the hope I shall be able to convince more hon. members of the necessity of supporting the amendment which we in the C.C.F. party have moved. Our amendment relates to the referral of the subject matter of this bill to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. I am afraid that some of the newer members in the house are not completely acquainted with the operations of this standing committee. It is understood, of course, that this committee would receive recommendations from farm organizations and interested organizations all across Canada as to what should be the subject matter of this bill.
I think we can very well see that if farm organizations are consulted, and if they are asked to prepare draft legislation that may relieve the problems confronting farmers all across Canada, we would have a bill which would meet the needs of agriculture today. One of the complaints which has been voiced by farm organizations against this bill is the fact that in drafting it initially none of the farm organizations in Canada were consulted. It is true, of course, that the farm organizations were later consulted with a view to improving the legislation. Indeed that, in my opinion, has been the purpose of this debate, and it is the purpose of my participation in it. I am hoping that by presenting the views of my constituents, and the views which I myself have as a practical farmer, this legislation may be improved upon for the benefit of the people of Canada.
We know that the Agricultural Prices Support Act was passed in 1944. We are aware also of the fact that it was the only legislation which agriculture had up until the present time. The members of the government have stated how useless this legislation was. The hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) admitted that the Agricultural Prices Support Act was just as bad as he claimed the agricultural stabilization bill is. We are, therefore, in the position of having
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization secured the best possible bill for the benefit of farmers. We know quite well that the agricultural stabilization bill, or any other measure that is passed this year, probably will be on the statute books for the next 15 or 20 years.
We in the C.C.F., and I must give full marks to my hon. friends in the Social Credit party, have been successful in achieving results so far. It was our suggestions at the resolution stage, along with the suggestions of farm organizations, which prompted the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) to make certain changes. The minister stated at page 2652 of Hansard for December 20, when he moved second reading:
However, concern has been expressed by members of parliament of this party representing rural constituencies-*
The minister then goes on to express the opinion that the wording of these clauses has led to a misunderstanding. I looked very carefully through the debate on the resolution stage of the bill, and I noted that the only comment made on the bill was made by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) when he stated:
I want to make the definite statement that we are proud of the proposed legislation-
I imagine that criticism from a government member must have cut the minister to the quick, and on that basis he introduced the amendments.

It has been officially stated by their farm spokesman, namely the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner), that they are going to support the bill. At the same time they have indicated that it is a bad bill. This is an indication that this once great party is again only attempting to play politics. They have agreed that this bill is so bad that it is going to harm the people of Canada and they are prepared to support it so that it can inflict harm on the people of Canada. If they were indeed taking the right view they would try to improve the bill. If they feel that the bill is not as good as the one which they themselves drafted, namely the Agricultural Prices Support Act, then I think they would be in duty bound as representatives in a democratic parliament to vote against it. However, again we have an indication that "soon" can mean very late'.
I want to make reference to a comment made by the former minister of agriculture to a statement made by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schulz). The hon. member

pointed out the very small amount that had been spent for agricultural supports over the period of years, and the former minister of agriculture went to great lengths, as he is capable of doing, to attempt to show that it had cost the government, in fact, a huge sum of money for stabilization under the old Agricultural Prices Support Act. I have the annual report of the Minister of Agriculture for the year ended March 31, 1957. The hon. member for Meadow Lake admitted that he was a better saxaphone player than he was a critic of this legislation but he concluded by saying he was going to support it.

With the objective of improving this legislation I, like many hon. members, took the opportunity during the Christmas recess of meeting with as many of my farmers and representatives of farm organizations as I possibly could. At one of those meetings held in Kindersley a resolution was passed giving me guidance and direction for my conduct in the house. I am going to place that resolution on record since it is quite brief. It explains the stand that the people in my constituency want me to take. The resolution reads as follows:
Whereas the agricultural stabilization bill fails to give any basic improvement to offset the declining position of agriculture, such as stating a definite cost-price formula upon which forward support prices could be based.
And whereas the government failed to honour their promise of consulting farm organizations in the drafting of the stabilization bill;
Therefore be it resolved that we oppose the bill as such and request that the bill be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization before a final draft is submitted to the house.
I think it is quite apparent that that resolution is the principle upon which I am debating. As I mentioned, that resolution was endorsed at ten meetings which I was able to hold during the Christmas recess.
I think we can safely assume, Mr. Speaker, that the objective of this agricultural legislation should be to provide a reasonable standard of living to the family style farm. I do not think it should be the intention of any farm legislation to provide a standard of living or a guarantee for the benefit of any regional or sectional interest in Canada. It should not apply only to Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia or Saskatchewan. We recognize the fact that agriculture is still Canada's basic industry. I assert that it is impossible to have a healthy nation without a strong, expanding agriculture. Let us measure this bill up against these qualifications.
We find that the western farmer is specifically excluded from any benefits that might result under the act. I do not know why we are excluded but, as reported at page 2187 of Hansard, at the resolution stage this was stated by the Minister of Agriculture:
The reason for this is not to interfere in any way with the operations of the wheat board,-
Just what kind of ghost are they trying to conjure up here, Mr. Speaker? The Canadian wheat board is approved by the great majority of Canadian western farmers. We also know that the Canadian wheat board is allowed to operate within the legislative program set down by this parliament. We have recently passed legislation for cash advances which are operated through the Canadian wheat
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization board. Can we, by any stretch of the imagination, assume that by including wheat, oats and barley we would in any way reflect on the operations of the Canadian wheat board or make it more difficult for them to operate? If there was conflict between the operation of these acts, surely it should have shown itself before now. The old Agricultural Prices Support Act included oats and barley and we did not notice any apparent conflict. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we recognize the fact that that conflict did not exist because of the inactivity of the previous government with regard to promoting any price supports for those products. I would suggest to the minister that he give serious consideration to this aspect of the bill, namely the inclusion of western wheat, oats and barley. It is just as important to agriculture to have western agriculture in a healthy condition as it is to have agriculture in any other area in a healthy condition.
At the resolution stage I pointed out to the minister some of the figures relating to the cost of production of wheat. In doing so I think I was able to prove to the satisfaction of all hon. members the necessity for some immediate program of assistance for western farmers. The principle of deficiency payments has been in part recognized in this bill and that is something that is being currently requested by farm organizations.
In this matter of wheat we can go back to the time of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, when that act was being adopted and call to witness the then hon. member for Lake Centre, who is now the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). He thought that wheat was an important subject because he said, as reported at page 5602 of Hansard for July 29, 1944, the following:
There is one other matter to which I wish to refer, and that is in connection with grain farmers. The grain farmers in western Canada today are not as well off proportionately, even taking into consideration present day prices, as other groups of farmers across this dominion.
There we have the present Prime Minister back in 1944 pleading for the grain farmer and, later on in the same debate, as recorded at page 5603 of Hansard, the then member for Lake Centre and the present Prime Minister stated:
I mention this for the purpose of asking the minister to consider raising the standard level of prices paid to the grain farmers to the end that our farmers in Saskatchewan may attain parity price or a reasonable price above that amount having regard to all the circumstances.
What a transformation we have from the battle that was being put up by the then member for Lake Centre to what is in the bill before us! We find even during the election campaign that the present Prime Minister

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization was reported in the Star-Phoenix of May 29, 1957 as having said while speaking in Saskatoon that any person who voted for a Liberal candidate in that election would be voting for a wheat policy which has proved ineffective, lacking in initiative and which has brought about the most serious situation western Canada has ever faced.
There is an account of the tragic circumstances which existed in western Canada and which are being completely ignored in this agricultural legislation today. I do not know what has happened in the period from 1944 through the election campaign of 1957 to date. I do not know what has changed the picture, with one exception, and that is the election of a Conservative government.
I do not think we should forget these statements made in the past. I think it is important that I, as the representative for a farming constituency, should put up the same battle for the farmers I represent as was put up by the former member for Lake Centre- I might say with equal justification. As has been mentioned, the objective of this legislation is to provide a reasonable standard of living for the farm family. Mr. Speaker, when Bill No. 237 was first introduced in the house and the members had an opportunity to see just what was in it, strong protests were raised both by the members of the C.C.F. and the Social Credit groups, as well as the farm organizations across Canada. As soon as I saw the bill I wondered who had drawn it up, or who was responsible for drawing it up, as it was quite evident that it was not drawn up by farmers. We have found out since that the farm organizations were not consulted in any way before the bill made its appearance in the house.
The first bill had no preamble, and proposed to establish a base price for a commodity by calculating the average price at representative markets for the three years immediately preceding the year in which the base price was established, and a floor price of 80 per cent of the base price was to be mandatory. However, the new bill carries with it a preamble, which I think is an improvement to the bill. The preamble states that it is expedient to enact a measure for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment, and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the cost of the goods and services that they buy. This partly meets one of the objections that I raised to the bill when I spoke on December 11. I said at that time that there was not a single word in the legislation which indicated that the farmer would get his fair share of the national income.
While the preamble says that it is expedient to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the cost of the goods and services that they buy, the explanatory note on page 2 states that in order to provide basic security to farmers guaranteed by legislation on key commodities, minimum floor prices of 80 per cent of the base price will


be mandatory. I claim that 80 per cent of the base price certainly is not what is required to put agriculture back on its feet. Surely if there is to be a fair relationship between the prices received by farmers and the cost of the goods and services they buy, they must get 100 per cent of their cost of production and enough besides that to enable them to live properly.
I do not suppose that anybody has worked out yet what the base price would be for any of these commodities for the ten years immediately preceding the year in which the base price is to be established. It might figure out at only 80 per cent of the cost of production, and certainly 80 per cent of 80 per cent would be of no great help to the farmers. The minister has complained that most of the speeches in the debate were setting out the position of the farmer financially, claiming that the government knew all these things and knew that help was needed to put agriculture back on its feet. If this legislation is not going to give them 100 per cent of parity we might as well throw it out and go back to the Agricultural Prices Support Act which the government found quite convenient to use very recently in the case of floor prices on sugar beets.
As far as I am concerned, I represent an agricultural constituency, and I am certain of one thing and that is that the farmers will expect me to fight for the kind of legislation which will put them back on their feet, and which will stop the exodus from the farms and prevent many thousands more farmers from going bankrupt. As far as I am concerned, if we are going to throw out the Agricultural Prices Support Act I want something put in its place that is going to do a job. I do not want any half-baked legislation with which the farmers that I represent are going to be very much dissatisfied. I want to see a support price set at a level that will ensure the cost of production and a reasonable profit. And if this is not done, it will be a denial of the farmers' due.
Can the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-ness) tell me of any other industry in Canada that would be satisfied to produce their commodities at 80 per cent of their cost and sell them at 80 per cent of their cost. Of course not, and nobody would expect them to do so, and if they were forced to do that they would soon go out of business. So I say, if the government is going to try and put agriculture back on its feet surely we can have a bill that will do just that. I wonder if the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had anything to do with the drafting of this bill, or who was responsible for it. It certainly does not look as though the Prime Minister .had anything whatsoever to do with it; perhaps he did not

even see it. But if he saw it, and if he had anything to do with the drafting, he has a lot to answer for; or at least a lot of words to swallow. For at least 13 years he has been talking inside and outside of this house, claiming that floor prices should be at a level which would ensure the cost of production and a reasonable profit. Now that he is Prime Minister of Canada is he backing away from the things that he advocated down through the years?
The Prime Minister has gone up and down the length and breadth of this country; he has spoken in every province and in almost every town in the dominion and he has been advocating those things for the last 13 years. Now I say let him back up the things he has been advocating and give us a decent bill.
I want to take the house back just 13 years, to February 4, 1944, when the Agricultural Prices Support Act was being discussed in the house. At page 192 of Hansard for February 4, 1944, the present Prime Minister had this to say:
Reference has been made in the speech from the throne to agriculture, but time does not permit my discussing that today, except to say that I believe in the principle of floor prices, but like hon. members who have already spoken I ask the government what level is to be set? Is it to be a price level in accordance with present prices and subsidies? Is it to be a level that will ensure the cost of production and a reasonable profit? If it is not, it will be a denial of the farmers' due.
That is just what I said a few moments ago. In stating what I did I can bring another good witness in the person of the Prime Minister again. Speaking on July 29, 1944, at page 5600 of Hansard, the Prime Minister had this to say:
In other words some will say that the bill will ensure parity prices.-
He was talking about the Agricultural Prices Support Act which was under discussion at that time. I continue:
-when in fact, there is nothing in the bill to indicate that parity prices will be the aim of the board in the price levels which it will set. This measure sets a floor price by an indirect method,-
That is what the present bill purports to do. The Prime Minister continued:
-that of permitting the board to go into the market and make purchases, but the level of prices at which the board will make those purchases is not indicated. The farmer understands floor prices to be prices set at a level which will assure him of a reasonable profit over and above his cost of production, although some consider them to be the same as parity prices.
Listen to this.
To be fair to the farmers of Canada, and not hold out to them hopes that may not culminate in action, the minister should set forth in this bill the principle that prices paid in respect of farm commodities shall be based upon cost of production and a reasonable profit.

That is exactly what we in the C.C.F. are asking the Minister of Agriculture and the government to do in this bill. I quote again from the Prime Minister:
That would not require his setting price levels today to be effective in the post-war period. But if this bill is to be anything more than the promise of a hope, there must be something in it to show that the prices farmers are to receive will assure them of reasonable cost plus a fair return.
A few lines farther down on the page the Prime Minister had this to say:
Under this legislation the farmers of Canada may hope that the price they are going to receive will be a fair one. And a year hence or two years hence may realize for the first time that under this legislation there is no mandatory requirement on the board to assure our farm population a fair return for products they produce.
That is exactly why we in the C.C.F. are insisting that this government do something more than hold out a hope to the farmer. Many of our farmers are desperate and I do not want to see this government hold out a carrot before their noses, hold out a promise before them which will only go part way toward solving the pressing need for prices which will ensure them their cost of production and, as the Prime Minister said so many times, "plus a reasonable return".
Therefore, I again plead with the Minister of Agriculture to let this bill go to the agriculture committee where we can have the farmers and the farm organizations come before that committee and try to bring forward a bill which will do the job which is needed.
I could say a lot more at this time, Mr. Speaker, but it would appear that we are coming close to the end of the debate and I hope that the minister will agree to let this bill go to the agricultural committee-

Before the minister speaks to close the debate I feel that I should like to take just a few minutes of the time of the house to express some of the reasons why, unless the minister brings in some fairly substantial amendments to the bill, we will not be able to support the motion for second reading. I must begin, Mr. Speaker, by saying that the bill as it now stands is unacceptable to the farmers and farm organizations of the country. Even if some of the amendments that have been suggested are implemented, it would still be unacceptable.
I take the position that I do for the reason that I represent a farm constituency. Over the years my people have asked me to work for parity prices, to work for forward pricing, to work for some marketing and pricing legislation that is based definitely on the cost-price relationship. They have asked me also to work for the protection of the family farmer, and to see to it that conditions are laid down so that he is not driven from the farm. They have asked me also, Mr. Speaker, to see what I could possibly do to ensure that we have in this country the kind of pricing and marketing legislation that will guarantee the farmers their fair share of the national income.
Having been given those instructions, I would not be true to my trust as the representative of an agricultural area in this country if I did not constantly work for those things. My group in the house thus far have spoken and have given the foundation reasons why these important things should be made a part of any farm legislation introduced here. I should like to speak for just one moment rather directly to the minister. He is a friend of mine. He comes from my own province, and he knows the situation out there. I feel quite certain that he has a knowledge of agricultural problems. I am quite certain that if he were given a free hand to do so he would try to introduce an agricultural prices support bill that would truly reflect the needs of the farmers in this country.
I am afraid, however, that the minister has been frightened by the adverse publicity that so many of the eastern newspapers have given at any mention whatever of parity prices. Unfortunately, he has been supported in his fear of parity prices by statements that have been made by the former minister of agriculture. I am very much surprised at that, especially in view of the fact that all during the election campaign Conservative candidates stated that they would do their best to have parity prices established in any farm legislation that came into this house. The parity principle itself is nothing to be

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
afraid of. I am surprised at grown men, men of experience and vision, coming into this house and saying that you cannot establish the parity principle without getting into the same trouble as the people in the United States have experienced.
I think that is foolish. After all, Mr. Speaker, there are many devices that could be incorporated into agricultural legislation which would prevent the subsidization of vast surpluses of unwanted goods. It is not necessary that parity, established as a principle in agricultural legislation, give rise to unwanted and unmanageable surpluses of food. There is, for instance, the technique of quotas for delivery.
Taking under consideration, for example, the supply and the demand situation at any period it would be a simple matter amongst the wheat growers of western Canada to adopt, for example, as the standard an average size productive unit which would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of 400 to 500 acres. If that were established as the comparative unit and if the minister were to suggest that deliveries from all such units of grain produced would be subject to the 100 per cent parity price, but units, for instance, that may be larger than that would not be able to enjoy the parity principle on all that they produce, I am quite certain that they could control the situation without having too great a bureaucracy to do it. I am afraid that he shows his fear of legislative responsibility or administrative responsibility. But I am just as positive as I am that I stand here that we could introduce into our situation the parity principle without building up unmanageable surpluses of food such as those which have been built up in the United States.
One of the reasons why we were anxious to see this bill sent to the committee for study was in order to see whether it would not be possible to find some such techniques and introduce them into the bill. We are not suggesting for one minute that we adopt the 100 per cent parity principle and have that apply to all of the production that could possibly be brought into being by farms of all sizes, whether they be individual, family or corporate farms. We are not suggesting that for one moment. But the fact that the government have shied away from parity and are now trying to deny that they ever had anything to do with it is, in my opinion, surprising in the extreme. It is because of the fact to some extent that the government has not included in this bill any suggestion that we adhere to the parity principle that we feel disappointed. We feel that unless some substantial amendment is brought in by the 96698-234
minister before second reading or is suggested at least before second reading is called for, we could not support the second reading of the bill.
We have taken the position that any legislation designed to stabilize the prices of agricultural commodities should base its operative clauses on the cost-price relationship. The farmers and the farm organizations for years have asked for that principle. Unless the minister announces that it will be his intention to amend the bill to make it clear that the base price shall be based upon the cost-price relationship, then I say that our group cannot support the second reading of the bill. That is a most important point. The way in which the thing is worded in section 7 of the bill now, just does not mean anything.
We in this group have also taken the position that the formula should be based on a fixed period. I cannot see how in the world you can do justice to the farmers of the country with a moving average, whether it be a three-year, five-year or ten-year average; no matter what average may be adopted. We suggest that the only fair method would be to have a fixed average period. It may be 1925-1929. It may be what some of the farm organizations have suggested, namely 1943-1945, or it may be ten years from 1947 to 1958. That would be perfectly satisfactory. If the minister were to suggest that he will bring in an amendment to establish that fixed period for comparing the cost-price relationship, then we would be prepared to give that amendment support. But unless he does so, it is just one more reason why we cannot support the second reading of the bill.
From what I have heard in the debate thus far I would judge that there are a good many people in the house who have the very erroneous idea that the western grain grower is an especially favoured fellow in this country. One of the reasons why we feel we must be severely critical of the bill is that it does not include western wheat, oats and barley growers. The western grain grower is left out of the calculation altogether, in spite of the fact that he is an extremely important part of the agricultural industry and in spite of the fact that it is that part of the industry which is at present so greatly depressed. Why in the world they would be left out, in the light of those facts, is something that I cannot understand.
I have heard a good many hon. members talk as if the western grain grower just puts in his crop, and a very big one, and has nothing else to do until he harvests in the fall. They seem to think that he just goes

That just is not so. I want to put on the record some facts to back up what I am now saying. Here is a table showing the size of occupied farms by acreage groups in the prairie provinces-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta-based on the 1951 census. The number of those over 1,119 acres or 1,120 acres would be comparatively small. Hence the extent of the farms is not so great as a good many people have been led to believe. From the figures I have given in the table, it is perfectly clear that the great bulk of occupied farms fall into those groups operating farms between 70 acres and 559 acres. That is, in the three western provinces or the three prairie provinces, of a total of 227,129 farms there were 172,156 of the size between 70 acres and 559 acres. Hence the average size of the grain farm in the prairies would certainly be much smaller than that which has been suggested here. The great bulk of them lie between 70 acres and 599 acres. I have not worked out the average size, but I would think that the average size family farm today in the west would not be 200 acres. During the past 20 years there has been an accelerated trend toward larger average farms per operator just as there has in eastern Canada.
I heard one hon. member a few moments ago talk about the reduction in the number of farms in Ontario. If I remember the figures correctly, he indicated that the number had been reduced by something like 12,000. That is a serious situation. If we are going to get into the same condition out west as that in which they find themselves in Ontario with regard to the number of farms, believe me it is going to be a serious situation for this country. We do not want that to happen. It has been stressed over and over again-and I want to add my voice- that we must do something to preserve the family size farm and to keep those people on the farm quite happy and prosperous.


It has been said that the western farmers are pretty well fixed and need little, if any, help. We have maintained over the years that our farmers all through Canada have needed realistic marketing and price legislation. Otherwise they simply could not maintain prosperity and they could not share equitably in the national income and in the prosperity enjoyed by other sections of our population. Perhaps the most significant figures in assessing this situation are those which will be found in another table showing the breakdown of dollar revenues earned per farm unit on the prairie provinces. Hon. members may be surprised, particularly those who think that if we do something to help the farmers we will be paying subsidies to just a few farmers, to see the picture presented by these figures. I have heard such sentiments expressed and I disagree. It is not so and I deny it emphatically and, to prove it is not so, I want to put these facts on the record. Whoever says such things is doing irreparable damage to the farmer.
Gross revenues per farm unit based on the 1951 figures, which year was one of the largest income years we have had for a long time-in fact farm cash income in 1951 reached the peak in Canada, then declining and has continued to decline until today- indicated that 124,839 farms in the three prairie provinces produced less than $2,500 per unit. Let that sink in; I am going to repeat it. One hundred and twenty-four thousand, eight hundred and thirty-nine farms in these three prairie provinces produced in 1951 less than $2,500 per unit. That was gross production and of that number 57,602 produced less than $1,200 per unit gross. They had to pay all their expenses in addition to a lot of difficulties which they faced in gambling against weather and that sort of thing. Let me go on: 42,603 produced between $2,500 and $3,749 per unit gross. All these figures I am quoting are gross and of course out of them they had to pay all their expenses including labour, cost of machinery, repairs, etc.
Twenty-five thousand and fifty units produced between $3,750 and $4,999 per unit. Twenty-four thousand and thirty-eight produced between $5,000 and $7,999 per unit and 9,224 only produced between $7,500 and $9,999 per unit. Now does that mean affluence? That gives the lie to those people who constantly say, "Oh, you fellows are exaggerating the situation." Nine thousand two hundred and twenty-four produced between $7,500 and $9,999 per unit gross and from there on the number producing anything more than $10,000 was very rapidly declining. Let me show you how.

Six thousand one hundred and eighty-four of all these farms in western Canada produced, gross, between $10,000 and $14,999 per unit. One thousand eight hundred and seventy-seven only produced between $15,000 and $19,999 per unit and 1,863 only produced over $20,000 per unit. So when people talk about where the subsidies might be channelled into the hands of a few, these figures give them the lie.

No one is putting up the claim that industrial workers are overpaid in relation to their cost of living, but on the other hand we do not want to forget that these figures do not include rents because the average farmer has his home, of some kind, somewhere on the farm. Most of them do not have such facilities as indoor toilets, running water and all that sort of thing. They certainly have to bundle up every time they go out, and we must remember that neither do they include that portion of the food which the farmer produces for himself. We know he is a little better off in that regard.
However, when we analyse the figures we see a number of the farmers in the western provinces who are producing a gross income each year which will give them little more than enough to keep one foot ahead of the sheriff and we must come to the conclusion, therefore, that something has to be done so that prices and marketing conditions for them are improved. That is what we have got to work for.
Someone has suggested that low income farm families be moved into the cities to find employment in industry. I do not believe
96698-234i
that such a suggestion becomes a person of average intelligence. The farmers of this country have established themselves, most of them after long and arduous work. I wish to speak particularly of those in the Peace river country. Those fellows went in there many years ago and carved out little farms and homes from the wooded wilderness. Many of them have been clearing the land by hand with axes and saws. Many of those old farmers went up there just after the first world war under some sort of military reestablishment scheme such as that of the soldiers' settlement board. Some have worked all those years since, struggling to clear their farms and to get them on a paying basis. They are just now beginning to get enough cleared and under real cultivation to be able to live.
Now these people have pioneered and have established their homes and they love the place. They are all they have in the world and to suggest for one moment that they should move out of their small farms and establish themselves in cities is just absolute foolishness. They do not want to move; they want to stay and to feel that they are contributing to the strength of this country by producing food. They do not want and they would not ask for help except for the fact that marketing conditions and prices are simply beyond their ability, individually or collectively in small groups, to control.
These are the things which I think my friend Ezra Benson, who has been quoted here so many times, had in mind when he suggested that the things the governments ought to be prepared to do for farmers are those things which the farmers cannot do for themselves. But the government ought to be prepared to do them, especially when it is the government which establishes all the other policies under which the farmers have to work and try to exist, such as tariffs, import duties and all that sort of protection to industry. Believe me, the farmer is the forgotten man in this regard and something has to be done to see that he has a substantially better chance.
As I said, some have suggested that low income farm families should move into the city to find employment in industry. In the first place we must consider if it is possible. No, it is not possible. They can be run off or chased out by allowing conditions to deteriorate to the point where they cannot stay on the farms any longer but that is not desirable. Suppose it were possible. I then appeal to the minister to consider this important point. Would the existing labour force in the cities and industrial centres like to see many thousands of Canadian farmers

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization move out of agriculture and into industrial jobs? Judging from the protests we have heard about immigration swelling the ranks of labour and taking away Canadian jobs I am quite certain that the workers in industry would not favour any such thing and indeed they would resist it with all their might especially since we have considerable unemployment already in the industrial centres without that condition from the farms.
Industry also requires skilled tradesmen. Farm trained people would not quickly qualify as such. It would take quite a long time and probably for some time they would swell the ranks of the unemployed and become just one more burden on government. Let us add to that the fact that automation is progressing very rapidly throughout all industry. Machines are replacing men so rapidly that industrial labourers will be hard put to it in the next few years to maintain themselves in jobs with take home pay. Why in the world, then, consider a suggestion that will swell the ranks of those who are already seeking doles or handouts.
I think it must become clear to the government and to any thinking person that the thing to do is to produce conditions that will maintain the farmers on the farms where they belong and where they want to be and help them to keep themselves going, and you do not have to be too generous with them even at that. There are those, of course, who make the claim that there are inefficient farmers. Of course there are, just as there are inefficient people engaged in any occupation. But just because a farmer happens to be a bit inefficient in his farm operations why in the name of common sense would you send him into the city to become a part of the rabble. That is a silly idea. I think the place for people who are somewhat inefficient might be right out there on the farms where they can do a bit of subsistence farming and contribute to their own upkeep. That is no argument at all against providing the proper kind of farm legislation.
I have come to the conclusion after long study of this situation that the real strength of agriculture in any country is the family farmer. It is not the corporate farmer or the big industrial farmer, that is the packer who goes out and buys a farm for the purpose of raising his own produce, that is the strength of our agriculture in this country. The real strength of agriculture is the family farmer who stays at it year after year, decade after decade, who trains his boys and girls to take their places on the farm to succeed him and keep things going to preserve the fertility of the soil that is so dear to them. If you look at the situation in England,


France or in any country that has become strong in agriculture you will find that it is the family farmer who is at the root of that strength.
In this fact there is a tremendous argument for introducing a farm bill that will give these people the proper protection and see to it that they receive their fair share of the national income. I say to you again that unless the minister assures us that there will be a firm declaration in the wording of the bill to the effect that one of its purposes is to ensure the farmer his fair share of the national income we will find it difficult to support the bill. We would like to be assured that the government and the board that will be set up under the bill are going to be guided by the farmer's estimated average cost of production rather than by the "have regard to" provision. We have had enough experience with that "have regard to" business before and it was not a happy experience by any means.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am glad that there is a Speaker who will restrain the desires of hon. members opposite to some extent.
I have read paragraph (d) of the submission made 10 days ago asking the government to make deficiency payments on wheat, oats and barley delivered to the Canadian wheat board during the crop year ended July 31, 1956. I am sure that they have in mind that the government would make available to the wheat board the money to make these deficiency payments. Why does the government not do something about it, now that they are purporting to deal with the situation in which agriculture finds itself today and about which the minister spoke so eloquently in the radio speech which he is proposing to have aired in western Canada on the 25th of this month.
Then, the wheat pool asked this:
(e)	That similar payments be provided on wheat, oats and barley delivered to the Canadian wheat board during the year ended 31st July 1957.
If the minister is going to deal with the situation in which farmers find themselves, where they are not getting a fair share of the national income, why does he definitely exclude that part of agriculture which everybody in the west knows needs deficiency payments to give those farmers a fair deal? I
3708	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the minister will not give any assurance that something is going to be done to give the government power to deal with these reasonable requests to which I have just referred in regard to deficiency payments to give our farmers a chance to meet their rising costs of living and to give them a chance to share in the prosperity this country has been enjoying for the last 10 years, then I do not see how I can support the bill.
The other day the minister made a great point of the fact that the basis of this bill was the cost of production. This does not satisfy me either. There was a clause written into the Agricultural Prices Support Act to the effect that the objective of that measure was to give the farmer a fair share of the national income, not to keep him on a basis where he just got his cost of production. Where would the Canadian economy or the Canadian people be without the food that the farmers grow? Surely when the farmers are doing this worth-while work they are entitled to a fair share of that national income.

I am dealing with what you are doing. You are in power. You are proposing to take out of the actual operative section of the bill this provision that that should be the objective of the board under that act. Why do you want to take it out of the bill? Is it because you do not want to be bound by it? By putting it in the preamble, of course you are not bound by it because it is just a recital which does not bind anybody. If it were put in the actual body of the act it would be the binding obligation on the board operating under that act to do its very best to achieve the objective of seeing that the farmer got a fair deal. Now this government in this bill proposes to repeal that provision which, when it was passed, the head of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture described as one of the most forward provisions that had been written in any act of parliament for many years. Now this government, after all the promises it made to our farmers, proposes to strike out of the law of the land that provision to which we could appeal with regard to getting fair payment for farmers first by supported prices and then by deficiency payments, under the law as passed by this parliament.
I should like to know-I think the minister should tell us when he speaks-why they strike a provision like that out of the law and only, after insistence by their own backbenchers and after protests from the farmers of this country, go so far as to


put in something that is not nearly as good. But they did not even put it in the operative section of the bill; they put it in the preamble. Why did they not put it in the operative section of the bill. Why put it in the preamble -if they wanted to do at least as well as the previous government had done when it passed the Agricultural Prices Support Act?
Mr. Speaker, we are meeting here after an election where the people on the farms indicated that they wanted something more done than had been done in the past for them, in order to give them a fair deal. The hon. gentleman's leader pledged himself to that objective on one platform after another all throughout Canada. He obtained thousands of votes on that basis. Now we are faced with a bill which repeals some of the basic rights of the farmers of western Canada and does away with rights they already have. It does not meet their needs in any way, shape or form. It purports to give them rights based on their cost of production but not to give them a fair share of the national income. I wonder how they think people will feel who really believed those promises of their leader. I wonder what the leader himself must think as he considers the promises he made upon which he received hundreds of votes throughout western Canada, when he sees that in this bill, which purports to be designed to give the farmer a better deal, the western farmers who grow grain and live by that means are forgotten men and are struck right out of the bill. Mr. Speaker, it is not good enough for the farmers of western Canada and it is not good enough for me.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this legislation is likely to be the most important of any to come before this house in the present session. While I have already on a previous occasion stated my views on the bill which is before us as originally introduced, I think at this time it is necessary to assess what progress has been made by this parliament in connection with this important legislation.
The situation with which we are faced at the present time is that the government has refused to accept the advice offered by the members of this group and of the Social Credit group to refer its subject matter to the committee on agriculture. On the other hand, we have been asked by members supporting the government, particularly in the speeches made yesterday, to accept this bill fairly well on faith, on the claim that they trust the powers which are granted to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and they are asking us to do the same.
The members of the C.C.F. group have stood four square for the acceptance of the

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
principle of parity prices for farm products for as many years as there have been C.C.F. members in this house. The members of the Social Credit party have also supported that principle. We are now being put in the position of having either to accept or reject the invitation from the government side to accept on faith a bill which does not meet the principle of parity prices for farm products.
The stand which we have taken in the past and which we are taking now is well supported by the farm organizations across Canada. It will not be necessary for me to document that support to any large extent because it has already been documented in great detail as the debate has proceeded. However, I am going to refer to one or two statements which have been put out by farm organizations and which deal with this legislation. Before I do so, however, I want to point out why it would be very difficult for either the members of this party at least and the Social Credit members-because apparently, by and large, the Liberal members are prepared to accept this bill on faith- to accept it in that way and why it would be difficult for the organized farmers to accept it on the basis of trusting the minister to administer the bill in such a way as to give the benefit of the doubt-if we can perhaps call it that-to the agricultural producer.
I have in my hand two statements which appeared in the Winnipeg newspapers on almost the same day. Both of them appeared during the Christmas recess, between Christmas day and New Years day. One of them was a statement, as reported by the Canadian Press, from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness). It appeared under the heading "Economic Outlook Good for '58, Says Harkness". The significant part of that statement is this. I may say this has a direct relationship to whether we can or cannot trust the administration of this bill to the minister in the hope that he can interpret as generously as possible what is contained in the bill itself. The minister is reported to have made this statement, and this is in quotation marks. If he did not use these words, he can correct them. These words refer to the question of prices of agricultural products and are as follows:
Regardless of circumstances that may develop, farmers will be assured prices almost as good as those secured in the past.
Almost on the same way there appeared a report of a speech delivered by the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, Mr. J. H. Wesson, under the headline "Farmers 96698-2354
Find Their Expenses Much Greater Than Their Income". The report goes on to say this:
He said, despite having delivered the equivalent of a better than average crop, farmers found their expenses for the year were much greater than their income. The reason was the continued increase in the cost of things farmers buy, while prices of farm products are declining.
If we take those two statements side by side, what do we find, Mr. Speaker? On the one hand the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool-there is no doubt that all other farm leaders will agree with what he had to say on that occasion-is claiming that the farmers are finding that their expenses are greater than their income, that their prices are still declining while their costs of production are still increasing. That is the situation with which we are faced and with which we have been faced for the last few years. In the face of that situation, what does the Minister of Agriculture undertake to do? He undertakes that regardless of circumstances that may develop farmers will be assured prices almost as good as those secured in the past. In other words, he is undertaking publicly to administer the bill in such a way that farmers will receive a little bit less than they have been receiving in the past few years, because he says prices will be almost as good. If you take "almost as good" as something which is bad you get something which is worse, and that is what the minister is promising the farmers of Canada-prices a little worse than they have been in the last four or five years.
That is a statement of the minister himself as reported in the press and, on the basis of that statement, no farm organization, no individual farmer and no member of this house who is interested in agriculture can accept it and leave this bill to be administered, on the statement of the minister himself, in such a way as to result in such prices. The minister has already publicly declared that it would be administered in such a way that prices will be a little worse than they have been in the last few years, and that is the point I wish to emphasize.
So we find the situation where the C.C.F. and Social Credit members are continuing their struggle to have written into the bill something which will assure to the farmers their fair share of the national income and something that will bear a direct relationship to or acceptance of the principle of parity prices.
Members supporting the government in their speeches yesterday-I do not wish to take the time of the house to quote them in detail-said on several occasions that they believed the farmers should receive their fair
3710	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization share of the national income. This was said by several members of the Progressive Conservative party yesterday. At the same time, however, they said they did not believe in parity prices as a method by which farmers could receive such fair share. That declaration, coming from government-supporting members, gives us even more reason for worry and concern as to the effect of this bill. If it is to be passed in this house in its present form and be left to the minister to administer in accordance with his public statement that it is his declared intention to administer prices in such a way that they will be slightly worse than they have been in the last few years, some further consideration must be given to this subject.
These two statements are completely inconsistent and contradictory. If they profess to believe that farmers are entitled to their fair share of the national income there can be no semblance of logic in saying at the same time that they do not agree with the principle of parity prices, because parity means equality. If in one breath you say you believe the farmer is entitled to equality and in the next breath you say you do not then you cancel out your own argument.
In my respectful submission, therefore, we cannot entrust the administration of this bill in its present form to the Minister of Agriculture having regard to his declared intention, nor can we entrust it to the advice of those members supporting the government because in either case it appears to me the whole question of the parity price principle will be sacrificed to the law of supply and demand.
We also have to consider the further proof of the minister's own statement when introducing the resolution preceding this bill, in which he stated very definitely that it was one of his motives in the bill to avoid any incentive to production. In other words, he intended to keep prices low enough to make sure they did not encourage any large volume of agricultural production. I would ask the minister how he squares that statement with the traditional policy of tariff protection in his own party. What is tariff protection if it is not an incentive for certain manufacturing industries to expand the production of certain manufactured articles? It was put there for that express purpose-as an incentive- and has remained on the statute books of Canada ever since.
The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), furthermore, is busily scurrying around trying to find ways and means to increase tariff protection', yet the Minister of Agriculture, who sits with him on the treasury benches, tells us it is all very well


and it is perfectly good to provide through our tariff structure an incentive to the manufacturer, regardless of whether that costs the Canadian consumer something- and it is costing them plenty, in fact, $400 million-but as soon as it comes to agriculture, he says, "No, we will not provide any incentive; we will allow the law of supply and demand to come in and make sure the farmer will always get a little less than his cost of production." That is the declared purpose and motive.
On the face of this we certainly have to go further than we have gone into this bill. Then we have to take into account the attitude of our Liberal friends on this side of the house because, after all, many of them represent agricultural constituencies. I should not say that many of them are from western Canada, because there are not many now, but there are a few. It is a matter of deep concern to me to note the attitude taken by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) yesterday, when he stated he would not be guilty of voting for a bill which would repeal the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Today he reinforced that statement very forcibly, and I congratulate him on his stand because it is a consistent one. However, while he was talking all that ran through my mind was what was said in this house a couple of days ago by the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) and the right hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner). When the hon. member for Rosthern made the statement to which I have just referred he was in effect accusing the other two members of being guilty of doing that very thing, because we find recorded at page 3610 of Hansard the following statement by the hon. member for Meadow Lake:
I hold in my hand the death warrant of any Conservative candidate running in a farming area in western Canada. I hold in my hand Bill No. 237. I would also say that I hold my own passport to this place after the next election.
There, Mr. Speaker, is a real expression of responsible statemanship; there is a member representing an agricultural community who regards this bill as a death warrant for any Conservative candidate running against him. Why? Because it is not good for agriculture. Furthermore, he regards it as a passport back to this house. I might advise the hon. gentleman that I think he will find he has got his passport and his death warrant all mixed up and I think it is a question of where he will end up after the next election.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was at that time pointing out the danger that was being run by the members of the official opposition in allowing their political partisanship to loom larger than the consideration of the principles of this bill. I mentioned that whereas the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) had stated in his address that he would not support this bill because of the fact it repeals the Agricultural Prices Support Act which in his opinion at least is a better act than the one foreshadowed by this bill, on the other hand the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner), who is the acknowledged leader of that party for the province of Saskatchewan at least, when speaking on December 20 last in this house on this bill as the lead off speaker for that party made a couple of statements which give rise to grave misgivings as to what the actual motives of that party are with regard to this legislation.
I think he was rather shooting from the hip at that time and being a westerner I suspect he would realize the danger of that practice unless you know in which direction the gun happens to be pointing particularly if you are making a cross hand draw as he was doing. In deciding how he was going to treat this measure, as recorded at page 2673 of Hansard of that date, the hon. member for Melville used these words:
I said a few moments ago that as far as I am concerned I am voting for the measure which has been brought in.
The hon. member was, of course, referring to Bill No. 237. He then went on to give some of his reasons, as follows:
Since it has been decided by the government to repeal the present measure

The Agricultural Prices Support Act.
-and bring this amendment bill forward I can only say there is nothing in it I would be particularly opposed to although I must comment that it does not do as much as the existing act does and I am opposed to it on that basis.
As usual, this is one of those sentences that starts off in one direction and ends up going in another but the only analysis one could make of that stand is that the hon. member believes that Bill No. 237 is not good and chiefly it is not good because it repeals the present Agricultural Prices Support Act which, in his opinion, can do more for the farmers than can the present bill. Then the hon. member concludes with the strange decision that because this bill does away with an act that is better than the bill, he is going to vote for the bill. Later on in the speech, of course, he clarifies the reason for that by saying-I am only paraphrasing-that he is
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization content to let this bill come forward and be adopted in order to let the farmers see how bad a bill it is and then he is going to go to the country and fight the government on the basis of a bad act.
We in this group feel that this is hardly the way to approach legislation as important to agriculture as this because, after all, if it is unsatisfactory legislation it is the duty of all members of the house-not only opposition members but all members of the house who have an interest in this subject-to do everything possible to improve it. I suspect that the hon. member for Melville was organizing a sort of game of cops and robbers. Here he had cast the terrible Tories in the role of a group of robbers who were going to swoop down on the farmers and take away a good act from them and thus give an opportunity to the Liberals to come rushing in from the other side, in the role of the cops to rescue the farmers. Of course what he failed to take into account was that the farmers for the past 22 years have had more experience with the cops than they have had with the robbers and at the present time they hardly know by which side they would rather be rescued.
What we in this group have been trying to do during the course of this debate has been to relate to what is now before us the express and considered desire of the farm organizations across this country with respect to farm legislation to see whether it measures up to what the farm organizations actually wish and also to see whether it measures up to what the party that is now in power pledged itself to do when it was in opposition and particularly during the course of the last general election. That is what I intend to do in a moment.
I have before me a large volume of representations from farm union locals across my constituency as well as outside the constituency and some submissions from the federation of agriculture in the various provinces much of which has already been put on the record and it would be redundant to put it on the record again.

However, I have two representative resolutions which I believe set out rather fully the attitude of both the federation of agriculture and of the farmers' unions in relation to what they expect this government to do with respect to farm prices.
I wish to read a resolution submitted by the Gilbert Plains local of the Manitoba farmers' union in my own constituency copies of which were forwarded to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Minister of Agriculture, the hon. member for Springfield
3712	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization (Mr. Schulz) and to me. Some of the hon. members from the west will know that this particular part of Manitoba is the area in which the farm unions developed the earliest and this is one of the largest and most influential locals in the province. They placed the matter before the government and members of the opposition in the words of the following resolution:
That whereas decreased farm income due to depressed prices during a time when other industries are prospering and the cost to the farmer is ever increasing, drastically affects the living standard of the farmer;
And whereas there appears to he no lessening of the price-squeeze pressure on the agriculture industry, therefore he it resolved:
(a)	That we urge the government of Canada to establish a price support program based on 100 per cent parity on all agricultural products produced and consumed in Canada; and be it further resolved
(b)	That the export prices on farm produce be negotiated and set by the government and farm organizations.
I turn to a copy of a night letter which was dispatched to the Minister of Agriculture on December 18, 1957, by the provincial board of the Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation, which reads as follows:
Your proposed price support legislation fails to assure the farmer of improvement in present financial position. It is our contention and was one of the main planks in your election platform and continuing policy (Hansard, April 8, 1941; March 23, 1953; March 12, 1956) that price support legislation should provide a formula based on a period of years when the income of the farmer was in fair relationship to other groups in the Canadian economy.
That pretty well sets out the point of view of both those major farm organizations. The minister is well aware of that because in both cases copies of these, or the originals, were sent to the Minister of Agriculture as well as to the members of the house. Lest the minister thinks that this farm organization does not mean business, listen to this press dispatch that was issued somewhere around January 1 this year. I am not sure of the date but it was very close to January 1. This appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, and reads as follows:
Two Manitoba farm leaders-in predictions for 1958-agree that Conservatives will lose considerable support in western Canada if proposed federal price support legislation passes in its present form.
May I point out that this was after the minister had offered those five amendments to which I shall make reference a little later on. I continue with the quotation:
James Patterson, president of the Manitoba farmers' union, and Percy Burnell, president of the Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation, both claim that the controversial price support bill is the most important matter facing the present government.


"The political future of government hinges largely on the price support bill," said Mr. Patterson. If it passes in its present form, it will have a detrimental effect on the government's position in western Canada.
This is borne out by the following statement by Mr. Burnell:
If in 1958 the farmer does not see an adequate degree of support, his present disappointment might well become resentment.
That sets out quite clearly that those farm organizations have not only placed before the government what their stand is on this particular question but they are prepared to follow it up by taking the appropriate action to see to it that the government is held to its pledges. In other words, they have pledged themselves publicly to keep the government honest, and we are trying to do the same thing on this side of the house.
I think that somewhere along the line the Minister of Agriculture will have to admit that his proposed legislation went off the tracks. When he introduced this legislation on December 11, I believe it was, he made a brave speech. It is all on the record and I do not need to quote from it. But he in effect told this house that the government had given full consideration to this question, had taken advice from the different sources from which he was going to take any advice and as much as said to the members of this House of Commons, which includes his own supporters, that this was the final word; this is what you are going to get whether you like it or not.
He did not get very far. He had hitched a very new shining engine to his farm train. Before he got to the next station the thing was derailed. The first thing he knew he was forced to bring in five amendments and put them before the house in a most unusual manner, a manner which was, of course, strictly out of order. If it had not been for the unanimous consent he received he could not have done it. Then he brought another bright, new, shining engine to the rescue, but it too went off the rails. He decided that what he needed was not a new locomotive but a new cowcatcher. Therefore, he hitched the preamble in front of the bill. He thought he was going to persuade the farmers that because he had put cost-price relationship in the preamble everything was going to be fine, because those who believe in parity prices are going to be satisfied that it means parity prices, and those who do not believe in parity prices, which includes more than half of his party and probably 90 per cent of it, are going to be satisfied that it does not mean parity prices. He thought he was going to satisfy everybody. The point I wish to

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
make is that when you try to satisfy everybody by deceiving them you usually end up by satisfying nobody. That is what happened.
I think what is needed now-and I propose this as assistance to the minister rather than criticism-is for the members of this house to put that train back on the rails again. There is a way in which that can be done. Before I come to that I want to set out what in my opinion are some of the things that have to be put in the new bill that I am going to propose to the minister. I think this pretty well represents the opinion of organized agriculture as well as the opinion of a large number of hon. members in this house. These things are needed in order to clear away all this wreckage for which the minister is responsible and the confusion which he himself has introduced by first introducing a bill, and then introducing some amendments and reprinting the bill which has no legal status, and confusing almost everybody who reads Hansard as to what is actually before the house now. On top of that, I must say the minister intends to bring in some more amendments.
As a matter of fact I will make him a small wager at the present time. I will bet him a bottle of the finest pasteurized milk that money can buy-and I will purchase it at a parity price, too-that before this discussion is over he is going to introduce some more amendments to this already amended version of the reprinted bill. There is a danger that it may create still further confusion. I suggest to him that what he should do is withdraw this bill entirely and introduce a new one, and that new bill should contain certain principles which I shall mention in a moment.
Before I do that, in order to put the matter formally before the house, I am going to move as an amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Springfield; the following:
That Bill No. 237 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the advisability of introducing at this session legislation making definite and statutory provision for parity prices for agricultural products at levels that will assure to producers their fair share of the national income.
I have placed this amendment before the house, and I would like to mention now what in my opinion are five necessary inclusions in this proposed new bill which would do a great deal towards meeting the desire of organized agriculture and certainly would clear away the confusion which has been created by the minister again in trying to introduce his bill in two separate parts.
In my opinion, a satisfactory bill should contain within it, first, the parity price principle, and not in the preamble but expressed
in the legislation itself, having legal and binding effect. Second, it must contain a price formula which will relate support prices in the bill to the parity price principle. Third, it must have a firm provision for assuring producers that they will get full value of any deficiency payments that will be made. Fourth, it must give the stabilization board authority equal to the responsibility they will carry for the price levels that are adopted. Fifth, it must treat producers in all parts of Canada on the same basis.
It would be obvious that the five points are designed to fill out the inadequacies in the present bill. If time permitted I would go over each one of them to point out how the bill at the present time does not live up to these five main principles but I see that my time is rapidly running out. Therefore, I shall have to conclude by making one final appeal.
This is not to the Minister of Agriculture. He has already spoken on two occasions at least and he will probably speak again before this is decided. But I do want to make a special appeal to the Prime Minister himself. After all the speeches that have been made on the subject the record is full of the pledges that have been made by the Prime Minister at one time or another in the house and outside of it on the question of parity prices for farm products. The hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell) only today placed on the record some of the statements made by the Prime Minister when he was sitting in the opposition indicating the attitude he then took, and supposedly his party along with him, on the question of parity for farm products.
I do not need to put any more quotations on the record. All farmers know, all members of the house know, everybody knows that the Prime Minister went across the country from one end to the other, spoke to agricultural audiences during the election campaign and pledged himself solidly that if he became prime minister he would introduce legislation to bring about parity prices for farm products. As a matter of fact, he spoke right in my home town and I heard him make the statement. Therefore there is no doubt as to what his pledge was.
The Prime Minister has seen fit to disregard or ignore the whole debate so far. There have been times when he has been present and has heard some of the views expressed and statements made from both sides of the house but he himself has not uttered one word either in defence of the proposed legislation or to state, as I think he should state, that this legislation is not adequate and therefore he is prepared to have
3714	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization the bill withdrawn and introduce something which does meet the pledges he made right across Canada. He has not done either the one thing or the other. He has ignored the debate. He has absented himself from the debate. He has taken the attitude that perhaps he is not involved in the debate and that any blame that will arise because of this inadequate legislation will fall upon other shoulders than his own.
I think that is quite unfair to the Minister of Agriculture. I see no reason why he should have to bail the Prime Minister out of all the pledges he made. I think the Prime Minister has a duty to the house, to the country and to agriculture to stand up in the house as Prime Minister and to defend his policies and the pledges which he made on behalf of his party. If he does not do that we shall have to assume that the members of the government are retreating from the position which they took before the election.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would point out to Your Honour that in my opinion this amendment is out of order on two grounds. The first ground is that in effect it is the same amendment as the one which we voted on this afternoon. The amendment we voted on this afternoon was to the effect that the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. The effect of this amendment is exactly the same, that the bill be not now read the second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of the house consideration should be given to the advisability, and so forth.
In other words, it is really just another means of saying what the previous amendment said, that the bill be not now read a second time and that something else be done about the matter. In the short time I have had I have not been able to find the citation covering this matter but I remember there is a citation which says that two amendments to the same effect cannot be moved in connection with the same bill. In addition, Mr. Speaker, citation 659 on page 229 of Beauchesne, third edition states:
An amendment purporting to approve the principle of a bill and at the same time enunciating a declaration of policy cannot be moved to the second reading.
That is exactly what this amendment does. Therefore on that ground, as well as on the other ground, I would maintain that it is out of order. The citation goes on to state:
It must oppose the principle of the bill.


This amendment does not oppose the principle of the bill which is that of introducing a form of price support for agricultural commodities. Therefore the amendment is out of order on that ground. The citation then notes:

Mr. Speaker, it is with a certain amount of trepidation that I speak on the bill. The farm lore of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) is likely to catch me up short. In addition, I have only had one letter from a farmer and he wanted a cold storage plant. The justification for the remarks I want to make has been established by the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Baskin) who appealed to the minister as someone he very much admired and respected to bring the pulpwood products of the farms of Ontario under the bill.
The constituency of Port Arthur takes a back seat to none when it comes to pulp-wood farming. Thousands of cords are cut there by men who own their own land and the question I raise for ministerial answer is the inadequacy of the 80 per cent floor based on a 10-year average for farm pulpwood if such pulpwood should come under the bill. I think the hon. member for Renfrew South made the point very well, that the price farmers have been getting for their pulpwood in general is much below the actual cost of pulpwood cut on pulpwood limits belonging to the various companies. Yet I could not see his point in hoping that farm pulpwood would come under the bill because if the price that farmers are getting at the present time for their pulpwood is low in relation to the actual cost of pulpwood from the other main source, a much bigger source, by the way, what good will the 80 per cent floor do them? Unless there is quite a drop

in the price of farm pulpwood there will not be any benefit and such a drop is hardly likely at the present time because no matter how much the production of the pulp mills may be restricted because of poor market conditions the fact still remains that the farm wood is cheaper for the pulp mills than wood from their own limits and it certainly is apparent in our area that they will continue to buy farm pulpwood. Therefore the price is likely to remain up and the product will therefore not come under the 80 per cent provision.
I should like to point out to the minister that I think any application of the bill to farm pulpwood is most unlikely to do much good and I should like to suggest to him and to hon. members from Ontario who have pulpwood farmers in their constituencies that these farmers are going to have to count on help under legislation of the Ontario provincial government, such as the farm marketing act. If the minister is going to heed the call of his several supporters who have requested the inclusion of pulpwood as one of the commodities, I hope he will give us a fairly complete explanation of how it would possibly work to the advantage of the pulpwood farmers of Ontario.
