speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the government is sincere in its desire to establish farm prices that will represent a fair relationship between the prices received by the farmers and the cost of the goods and services they have to buy, then I would think they would welcome advice from any and all farm groups and representatives. If this is so, then there will be no objection to including some of the recommendations of these organizations when they are all in favour of parity prices.
However, if the Conservative Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) believes that Bill No. 237, already amended in a number of instances since it was first introduced, is the answer to solving the farm problem, then there is no need to listen to representations from farm organizations or their representatives. It may well be that the Minister of Agriculture agrees with his colleague, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), who spoke before the amendments to the first draft of the bill were introduced and who said, foolishly I think, as reported on page 2290 of Hansard'.
I want to make the definite statement that we are proud of the proposed legislation, as proud as we are of the legislation we have put on the books to date.
I suggest his statement was foolish in the light of the amendments that followed but no more unrealistic than the bill that his

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
minister had introduced. I understand the hon. member for Marquette comes from a predominantly farm riding and I am told that when he returned to his constituency it was brought to his attention that hero worship of the party is O.K. in its place but that it has no place when the welfare of the farmers of Marquette riding is at stake. I am told that the hon. member was so informed at a meeting of the farmers.
For a moment let us take a look at the situation in the rural areas of Ontario. The problems of northern Ontario and the riding of Timiskaming in particular are the same as the problems throughout Ontario. In his election booklet the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to the plight of the farmers and had this to say:
The farmers' share of the national income has gone down in the last eight years by some 6 per cent and the services that the farmer has to buy have increased by 20 per cent. Furthermore, there has been a continuing reduction in the farmers' share of the consumer dollar, from 59.3 cents of the dollar to approximately 50 cents today.
I suggest that since this statement was made the drop has continued to well below 50 cents. It is recognized that a loss of income of 6 per cent in eight years and a rise in the cost of production by 20 per cent can only result in the abandonment of the family farm with the farmer moving into the urban centres to swell the ranks of the unemployed. Farmers are a land conscious people. They will suffer many hardships to establish their farms. This is particularly true in northern Ontario where not much over 60 years ago farmers went in, cut down the trees and established themselves on farms on which many of them still live today.
The farm family, the husband, wife and children, have their chores to do. If one is on a dairy farm, the cows demand the same attention morning and night, seven days a week. Yet a good many of my friends on farms will suffer from the strain of long hours, the whims of nature, the uncertainty of markets and an irregular income because they are devoted to the land. However, the farmers of Canada will only subsidize our agricultural economy for so long. Perhaps they have waited too long, it is not for me to say. But the fact that 1400 farms support only 400 fulltime farmers in my own riding indicates that time, for our farm population, is running out.
Perhaps the government today realizes that the farm population now comprises only 14 per cent of the total population. This farm population has been divided into many various farm organizations and into as many as 80 commodity groups. The government may think that this large number of divisions makes the position of the various commodity
groups that much weaker. It is true that in years gone by they have gone their selfish way. However, today they are united in a common front demanding the principle of parity prices. It has not been possible for the rural press, the manufacturing or financial interests, or even some political parties to divide the farmers in their adherence to the principle of 100 per cent parity prices. Each organization is asking for a fair price-cost relationship in so far as their products are concerned. The farmers, in adopting the principle of parity prices, are presenting a united, solid front.
Why then has the present government not given parity prices for agricultural products. I agree with those who say that farm products should include pulpwood from farms, timber and Christmas trees. It cannot be said that the Prime Minister does not understand the principle of parity prices. He campaigned throughout the rural areas on this platform. It is no secret that some of the candidates running on the Conservative ticket did not endorse this program. Obviously the Minister of Agriculture did not approve of parity prices, so we have this bill which appears to be unsatisfactory to all farm people with whom I have come in contact. One of the main excuses for not putting the principle of 100 per cent parity in the bill is the results of the farm program developed in the United States.
Mr. Benson, the United States secretary of agriculture, has become a great leader in the eyes of our new Minister of Agriculture. It seems surprising to me that a government which opposes trade and financial investment coming from the United States will, at the same time, accept the results of a farm program with which Mr. Benson has been experimenting, and which he calls parity prices. Recently the secretary of agriculture has presented to congress suggestions for changing parity prices. He has run into grave difficulties, I suggest, for the simple reason that his primary purpose in establishing parity prices was not to keep the small farmer on the farm but was rather to serve other interests.
In his report he made certain claims about the cost of this program in the United States similar to some of the claims that have been made in Canada over the years when this program has been opposed. In discussing these proposals one by one Chairman Ellender objected to the statements that were being made concerning the amount of money that this plan was costing.
I should like to mention some of the things that were included in the cost of the program, but were finally discarded because obviously they did not come under the farm program
3724	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization in the United States. These moneys were not used to subsidize farm prices. Such things as money for school lunches, food for troops and disaster relief were included in the charges against the price support program. Such things as disaster relief and school lunches certainly cost money, but by no stretch of the imagination could anyone say that parity prices did not work because expenditures of this type were charged against the program.
We all know that Mr. Benson wants to make some changes in that program. If the minister is going to refer to Mr. Benson, I would suggest that he take a look at the recent developments before using Mr. Benson and his plan as an example of the philosophy that "It won't work because it did not work there." We understand that the United States program must have cost money. Obviously there is a cost when any product is subsidized. Sometimes we have had products subsidized which we did not want subsidized, and there is one that affects me to some extent and one that probably cannot be justified any better than the demand for price supports under certain agricultural products.
While in Canada our farm prices were dropping and costs were rising in the United States, by using this plan, we find as reported in the Christian Science Monitor that prices received by farmers have been running 3 per cent above a year ago; surpluses have been cut; farm real estate is at an all time high and three-quarters of the United States farms are owned by the people who operate them. Farmers' debts total only 11 per cent of their assets.
In my particular area the debts on farms are again becoming a problem. We find that the farm loan board is now pressing for payment of overdue loans. Farmers are finding it increasingly difficult to make even interest payments on these loans.
I too visited some of my farm people at Christmas. In northern Ontario, and particularly in my riding of Timiskaming, a great number of commodities are produced. It is not safe to say that one commodity is the main one. I would assume that dairy products probably rank first in dollar value, but there are large sections producing beef, pork, eggs, butter, cheese, whole milk, pulp and Christmas trees. All the things, with the exception of fruit, that are produced on the farms in southern Ontario are produced in that area. Each one of these commodity groups have particular problems of their own. Many of these problems are not going to be solved by the passage of this legislation. However, all these groups are united in their organizations and in their demand for a fair

price-cost relationsnip. They all know that no matter what products they are producing, if it costs them more to produce a product than they get in return for that product then they are not going to be able to succeed.
The principle of parity prices has not been adopted in many industries, but it has been adopted in one with which I am familiar. The commodity group in my riding that is the best organized is the whole milk producers. These whole milk producers have been organized for quite some time. They have been able to negotiate their price; they have some control over the amount of the product that is going into the markets. It is true that they have been assisted by legislation which, by their militancy, they were able to have passed. Other farm groups have not been able to establish these rights, nor do they have the same strength in bargaining. The milk producers have been able to establish parity prices worked out on a formula which they agree probably is not the best one, but at least it is a formula. Hence they know that when their costs go up, then also the price of their product goes up.
It has a definite relationship. It is worked out and negotiated and the farmer is able to look ahead from one day to another and find out exactly how much money he is going to have to spend. If it can be done for the milk producing industry through the Ontario whole milk league, and if they are able to negotiate this kind of contract, I certainly see no reason why the federal government cannot put on the books legislation to allow the farmers to establish a relationship between their cost of production and sales, not only for the commodities which are named but for all commodities so that everybody engaging in that industry will know exactly how much money they can count on and how much money they are going to have.
Many of the people who do not live on a farm are never too sure just how much a farm costs. It is true that there are farms in parts of the country that are very cheap. They are farms that you could not possibly live on. It is generally assumed in Ontario that a milk producer is in a fairly enviable position. If you want to buy a dairy farm in Timiskaming today with a four-can quota, the cost would probably be $25,000 and that would be a 160-acre farm. The cost of 20 cows at $250 each would be $5,000. A barn equipped with the latest equipment so that you could eliminate the problem of labour would cost $10,000. Dairy equipment for a dairy farm with a four-can quota would cost approximately $3,000. A farm house that would meet the needs of the day in a rural area would cost approximately $8,000.

The farmland, if you bought it separately, would run about $50 an acre, or $18,000. Hence your farm would cost you fairly close to $40,000 equipped to handle four cans of milk a day. Four cans of milk a day-and milk is considered to be a fairly good income commodity-would bring an income of approximately $16 per day and for 365 days the amount would be $5,840.
Obviously for anybody who had $35,000 or $40,000 to spend, even in that commodity where we consider we have established some form of parity formula, to those who do not live on farms and have no great love for farming I would suggest that it would be a bad investment where you get a gross income of less than $6,000 on an investment of approximately $40,000. Besides that, the cows must be milked every day. They must be milked morning and night. There will be no time off. It would allow you to have enough equipment so that you will not have to hire help but it means that you will be tied to the farm morning, noon and night. If this is true of one commodity that works on a parity formula, how is it going to work for those poor people who are obliged to exist in that market of dog-eat-dog?
If we suggest that because we do not want to establish huge surpluses, we cannot afford to put in parity prices, then let us consider the one time when we came the closest we have ever come for years and years to establishing a parity price in Canadian agriculture and that was in the years from 1943 to 1951. For those who live on a farm were not those the best years they have ever experienced? That was the time when the cost of production came the closest it has come in years to the selling price of their commodities. Yet we did not find the farmer going out and buying more land or producing huge surpluses. With the farm that he had he found that he was getting only enough money to live on, and it was only in those days.
I remember being in Grey county only a few years ago and talking to a farmer there. He said to me, "This is the fifteenth tractor I have bought and this is the first one I have never been able to pay cash for." He said, "I am now farming five farms of 160 acres and I am going more in the hole every day. Every time I have less money than I need to live on I go out and buy or rent another farm and try to produce some more". The more he produced, the worse the condition became and he had reached the stage where he could no longer pay for his tractor.
That is happening in many areas of Ontario. It is happening today, I am sure, in most of the areas of Canada. But in 1951, when we were probably the closest we had ever
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization come to parity the farmers in my area at least were painting their barns. They were doing repairs to their houses. They were buying some equipment. They were living on their own farms and producing only the amount they needed to get along.
I am satisfied that if we had that parity established and could establish it with this bill, the situation would be improved. I see no reason why we should not give our Canadian people a fair break. The labour people have told you that they are not opposed to it. They want the farmer to get enough money to live on so he can buy the production that the farmer does buy. He is a very heavy consumer and he buys this production from my friends in the factories who are manufacturing them. When the farmer has no money he is not buying and then my friends are unemployed; and there are many of them unemployed today because the farmer is not buying. When they have not any money, they in turn do not buy the best cuts of meat. They do not buy butter and they do not buy the other things that the farmer has to sell. That is the only place where the working people can cut down, namely on food, and that is where they cut down first. So the prosperity of the farmer is important. I see no reason why the government should not give them prosperity on the farm. Prosperity on the farm will result in more employment in Ontario and certainly a much more happy and stable farm and agricultural community which in turn is a large consumer.
I received a letter the other day. Everybody seems to be getting letters. I received one which I do not want to read in particular, but I should like to refer to it. It came from a farm meeting. I should like to refer to one amusing thing. I had a farm candidate opposing me in the last election and the same candidate is opposing me in this coming election. He happens to be a Conservative. He also happens to be a member of both farm organizations and a well known farmer in that area. According to my information, he attended this meeting and they discussed the bill clause by clause. I sent them copies of both bills. They discussed the new one and the old one and they discussed the reprinted one. When they were finished discussing it they called on this particular gentleman to give what his opinion of the bill happened to be. Incidentally, most of the farmers at that particular meeting would be supporters of mine, so they gave him the opportunity to present his side of the argument. I should
3726	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization like to tell the minister that he did not support the bill but said that it was not satisfactory in its present form and should be amended.
I suggest that anybody who is close to agriculture can have no qualms whatsoever about giving the farmer a fair deal. If all farm organizations want parity prices, then why in the name of thunder should the House of Commons oppose them? I do not see any reason why we should have any Objection unless there is an ulterior motive and I might suggest it is this. The Searle Grain Company put out a pamphlet which I seldom ever read. However, I read this one and it sounds a bit like The Rural Scene which says such things as this.
The principal factor in the cost of everything we buy is the cost of labour. The unions have grown so powerful that they can practically dictate their own wage rates.
Then it goes on to say this. I was a union organizer and this is not true, I can assure you:
Employers have long since given up all thought of resisting their demands.
Then this pamphlet continues in a similar vein. It was either responsible for the drafting of this act, because they use the same words, or else the act was responsible for the writing of this pamphlet. It is the only organization of which I have read which is in support of this bill. If the grain companies opposed it I could not care less, but I do know that the people in my area who are on the farms, and mine is a mixed farming area which is quite exceptional and is known all over Ontario as the little clay belt, have dropped from 1,400 to 400 farms. Unless we do something about it the only people who will be left on the farms will be people who are working in the towns, and I suggest that we should go ahead and do something about this. If the minister has amendments to make then I certainly suggest when he speaks he should present them and we will be quite happy to have a look at them.

speechtext: As far as the Liberal members' criticisms of this bill are concerned I must say they have been very mixed. Of course it is difficult to tell just what their criticisms are, as it was difficult to tell what they were going to do or what they wanted. All I can do is take the general line of the criticism of the Liberal party, put forward by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) and which was followed by certain other members of that party. That criticism essentially boiled down to the allegation that this bill is no better than the Agricultural Prices Support Act, which has been on our statute books now for some eleven years, and that it might not be as good-

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I think if the members of the party opposite were to go out and speak to almost any farmer in this country in connection with this matter they would find very little agreement with that point of view, because it is quite apparent that this bill has many advantages over the Agricultural Prices Support Act and it differs from that act in many important respects. I have mentioned four of them before, and I do not wish to be repetitive as many of the hon. members have been and to prolong this debate-

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: What are you doing now?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The four very important differences between this legislation and the old are firstly that this bill provides for a mandatory floor price at all times on nine key commodities. The act which is presently on the statute books provides for no mandatory floors of any kind. Secondly, this bill provides for forward pricing. It has provided that a guaranteed annual price

be set for any commodity and this shall be in effect for the following twelve months, which puts the farmer in a position where he at least knows the minimum price, which he is going to get for the following twelve months.
